title: Dividing and Developing Land in Washington: Which Process You Are Actually In
titleTag: Dividing Land in Spokane County, WA | Justin D. Leigh
description: Which process your project actually falls under in Washington: boundary line adjustment, short plat, full subdivision, or binding site plan, plus ADUs, condominium conversion, and Columbia River Gorge review.
lede: You own five acres outside town and want to carve off a piece for your daughter. Or you have a corner lot and a contractor who says you can put two small units behind the house. Or you are buying a building downtown and the seller mentions, late, that it needs to be condominiumized before the sale closes. Every one of these is a different legal process with different triggers, different timelines, and different people deciding, and the most expensive mistake is starting down the wrong one.
intro: Washington puts the division of land under one chapter, chapter 58.17 RCW, and then exempts a surprising amount from it. The practical work at the start of a project is almost never about the merits. It is about correctly identifying which track you are on, because the track determines whether you are looking at a two-month administrative sign-off or a two-year public process.

sections.heading: The threshold question: how many lots, and are you making a new one

paras.p: The statute draws its first line by counting. A subdivision is the division or redivision of land into five or more lots, tracts, parcels, sites, or divisions for the purpose of sale, lease, or transfer of ownership. A short subdivision is the same thing into four or fewer. That single number is what separates the long process from the short one.

The ceiling moves, though, and it moves locally. Cities and towns may raise the short subdivision maximum to nine lots by ordinance, and counties planning under the Growth Management Act may do the same inside urban growth areas. So the answer to whether your six-lot project is a short plat is not in the state statute. It is in the local code, and two neighboring jurisdictions can answer it differently.
The second question is whether you are creating a new lot at all. If you are not, chapter 58.17 RCW may not apply to you in the first place.

sections.heading: Boundary line adjustments: moving a line without making a lot

paras.p: The exemption people most often need is in RCW 58.17.040(6). A division made for the purpose of alteration by adjusting boundary lines, between platted or unplatted lots or both, which does not create any additional lot, tract, parcel, site, or division, is exempt from the subdivision requirements.

There are two conditions buried in that sentence and both of them bite. No additional lot may be created, which means a boundary line adjustment moves lines between existing lots and never adds one. And the adjustment may not create a parcel with insufficient area and dimension to meet the minimum building site requirements. Shaving a strip off a nonconforming lot to help a neighbor can leave the first lot unbuildable, and a planner who notices will reject the application.

When it works, it is the cheapest tool in the chapter. It is also the one most often done casually between neighbors with a handshake and a surveyor, and then discovered years later by a title company that will not insure it.

sections.heading: Short plats and full subdivisions: the same project at two speeds

paras.p: A short plat is the map or representation of a short subdivision, and in most jurisdictions it is an administrative decision. Staff review it, conditions attach, and it is recorded. There is usually no public hearing, which is why projects get designed to fit under the lot count.

A full subdivision runs in two stages. Preliminary plat approval is the decision that matters, because that is where the conditions are set: roads, utilities, stormwater, dedications, open space, frontage improvements. Final plat is the ministerial confirmation that you built or bonded what you were told to build. People focus on the final plat because it is the one that records, but by then every term has already been fixed.
The conditions are the real cost of a subdivision, and they are negotiated during preliminary review. That is the moment to have someone reading the local code against what staff is asking for.

sections.heading: Binding site plans: the commercial and condominium track

paras.p: A binding site plan is a drawing to a scale specified by local ordinance that identifies streets, roads, improvements, utilities, and open spaces, carries the limitations and conditions the local government imposes, and contains provisions making development conform to the plan.

It matters because of two more exemptions. Divisions of land for industrial or commercial use are exempt from the subdivision chapter where the local government has approved a binding site plan, and so are divisions for the purpose of creating condominiums where a binding site plan has been approved. For a commercial project or a condominium, the binding site plan is often the entire land use path, and it replaces the plat rather than supplementing it.

sections.heading: What vests, and the exact moment it does

paras.p: Under RCW 58.17.033 a proposed division of land is considered under the zoning and land use ordinances in effect on the land at the time a fully completed application is submitted. That is the vesting rule, and it is genuinely protective: once you are vested, a later code amendment does not reach back and change the rules on your project.

The weakness is in the phrase. The statute does not define a fully completed application. It says the requirements shall be defined by local ordinance. So the single most consequential date in a development project is governed by a local checklist, and an application that is missing one item on that checklist is not an application at all for vesting purposes.
This is where projects quietly lose. A developer submits in March, assumes they are vested, learns in June that the submission was incomplete, and by then the code has changed.

sections.heading: Accessory dwelling units, and what the state now requires

paras.p: Washington has moved the floor under local ADU regulation. Under RCW 36.70A.681, cities and counties planning under the Growth Management Act must allow at least two accessory dwelling units on all lots in zoning districts within an urban growth area that allow single-family homes, in any of three configurations: one attached and one detached, two attached, or two detached.

The section also removes several of the tools local governments used to make ADUs impractical. A jurisdiction may not require the owner to live in the ADU or in another unit on the lot, which is the restriction that historically killed the most projects. Impact fees on an ADU may not exceed fifty percent of what would be imposed on the principal unit. Parking requirements are constrained near major transit stops and on smaller lots. And an ADU must be permitted on any lot meeting the minimum lot size for the principal unit.
What this does not do is override every other requirement. Setbacks, height, lot coverage, critical areas, and utility capacity still apply, and outside urban growth areas the picture is different.

sections.heading: Condominiumization: dividing the building rather than the ground

paras.p: Converting a building into condominium units is not a subdivision of land in the ordinary sense, and it runs through a different body of law. Common interest communities in Washington are governed by the Washington Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act, chapter 64.90 RCW, with older condominiums still touching chapter 64.34 RCW.

Two things surprise owners. The first is the document load. A condominium is created by a recorded declaration and a survey map and plans, and a developer selling units owes a public offering statement with disclosure obligations attached to it. This is drafting work, not form-filling.

The second is that conversion of an occupied building carries tenant protections, including notice requirements, and those are not waivable by agreement with the buyer. If the building has tenants, the conversion timeline is driven by their rights, not by the closing date.

On the land use side, remember the exemption above: a division for the purpose of creating condominiums is exempt from the subdivision chapter where a binding site plan has been approved. Getting that approval is usually the local piece of a conversion.

sections.heading: Variances, conditional uses, and rezones

paras.p: These are not division processes. They are relief from, or changes to, the rules that apply to a parcel, and they frequently run alongside a plat.

A variance asks to depart from a dimensional standard because of something about the property itself. A conditional use asks permission for a use the zone contemplates but does not permit outright. A rezone changes the classification and is legislative in character. Who decides each one, and whether that decision is a recommendation or a final determination, is set by the local ordinance and varies considerably.
The deadline to challenge any of them, once a decision issues, is short and unforgiving. That is its own subject, and I have written about it separately.

sections.heading: The Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area

paras.p: If your property is in Clark, Klickitat, or Skamania County, there may be a second government in your permit.

The Columbia River Gorge Compact, ratified by Washington at chapter 43.97 RCW, created the Columbia River Gorge Commission as a bistate body with Oregon. The Commission reviews major development proposals and new residential construction within the scenic area, may disapprove development it finds inconsistent with the purposes of the compact, may disapprove local land use ordinances that do not conform, and may enact land use standards itself where a county does not.

The practical consequence is that a project there answers to the county code, the National Scenic Area Management Plan, and a commission whose standards are scenic, cultural, natural, and recreational rather than merely dimensional. Applications that would be routine a few miles east are not routine inside the boundary.
I hold bar admission in both Washington and Oregon, which matters here more than it does almost anywhere else in my practice, because the Gorge is administered across the state line by a single body.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The wrong process. A project designed as a boundary line adjustment that actually creates a lot is not a boundary line adjustment, and the application will be rejected after the survey is paid for.
Vesting assumed rather than confirmed. The submission date only protects you if the application was complete under the local definition on that date.
Conditions accepted at preliminary plat without reading them. Frontage improvements and dedications imposed at that stage are the budget.
Discovering the Gorge boundary late. It does not follow county lines or the river bank, and the parcel either is inside it or is not.
Starting a condominium conversion with tenants in place and a fixed closing date.

sections.heading: Why this is lawyer work

paras.p: Most of this is reading. Someone has to read the local code against the state statute, determine which process the project actually falls under, confirm what a complete application requires in that jurisdiction, and read the conditions before they are accepted rather than after. None of that is adversarial and most of it happens before anyone disagrees with anyone, which is exactly why it is cheap to do early and expensive to fix later.

sections.heading: About my practice

paras.p: I am an independent attorney in downtown Spokane, at 601 W. 1st Ave., Suite 1400, admitted in Washington and in Oregon. Land use, subdivision, and development work is a regular part of my practice alongside real estate transactions and litigation, business and regulatory work, and civil litigation. I handle short plats, boundary line adjustments, subdivisions, binding site plans, condominium creation and conversion, ADU and infill projects, variances, conditional uses, and rezones, and I take Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area permitting, where my Oregon admission is directly useful. I represent clients throughout Washington.

sections.heading: If you are planning a division

paras.p: The useful first conversation is short. What do you own, what do you want to end up with, and which jurisdiction is it in. From those three answers it is usually possible to say which process applies, roughly how long it takes, and what the real cost drivers are, before you have spent anything on survey or design.

title: AI Governance for Law Firms: Client Confidentiality, Vendor Terms, and What to Write Down
titleTag: AI Governance for Law Firms, Client Confidentiality | Justin D. Leigh
description: Whether a legal AI tool can hold client confidences under RPC 1.6, which vendor terms decide it, what belongs in a written policy, and how verification becomes a workflow instead of an instruction.
lede: Most firms I talk to are somewhere in the same place. Someone is already using a chatbot, nobody has written anything down, a vendor has been in touch about a platform that costs more than the firm spends on research, and the managing partner has a vague sense that this should have been addressed six months ago. That is not a technology problem. It is a governance problem, and it is tractable.
intro: This piece is for lawyers and firm administrators rather than clients. I have written separately about what clients should ask their lawyer about AI use. What follows is the other side of that conversation: what a firm actually has to decide, in what order, and what the decisions cost.

sections.heading: The decision you have already made by default

paras.p: Every firm has an AI policy. Most of them are unwritten and the policy is "whatever individual lawyers decide to do, without telling anyone." That is a position, it is just not a considered one, and it is the one with the most exposure, because the firm carries the obligations whether or not it knows what is being done in its name.

The obligations are not new. Competence under RPC 1.1 has always covered the tools you choose to use. Confidentiality under RPC 1.6 does not change because the disclosure is to a server instead of a person. Supervisory duties under RPC 5.1 and 5.3 reach the work of people and resources a lawyer directs. Nothing about AI required a new rule in order to be governed.
The reason to write a policy is not that the rules changed. It is that an unwritten policy cannot be supervised, and supervision is the actual duty.

sections.heading: What a usable policy contains

paras.p: Short ones work better than long ones, because long ones are not read. A policy that fits on two pages and is actually followed beats a twenty-page document that lives in a shared drive.

It needs to answer five questions. Which tools are approved, and who approves a new one. What categories of information may be entered into which tool, stated concretely enough that someone can apply it at four in the afternoon. What has to be verified before it leaves the office, and by whom. What gets recorded, so that a question six months later has an answer. And what happens when someone gets it wrong, which should be a reporting path rather than a penalty, because a policy that punishes disclosure produces silence.
Notice that only one of those five is about the technology.

sections.heading: Can an AI vendor hold client confidences? The terms that decide it

paras.p: When a firm evaluates an AI product, most of the meaningful diligence is contractual rather than technical. The questions that matter are where the data goes, who can see it, whether it trains anything, how long it is retained, what happens on termination, where it is hosted, and what the vendor is permitted to do with it in the gaps.

The gaps are where the problems are. A term that promises your data will not be used for training, and then permits use for "service improvement" or "any other lawful purpose," has given the promise back. A default-on data sharing setting is a different product than the same product with it off. An indemnity that is capped below the cost of a single confidentiality incident is a number, not a protection.
This is ordinary contract review, and it happens to be work I do. It is also work most firms skip, because the agreement arrives looking like a click-through and gets treated like one.

sections.heading: Verification has to be a workflow, not an instruction

paras.p: The failure that produces discipline is uncritical reliance on an output that was never checked. Telling people to check is not a control, because the moment of risk is the moment someone is in a hurry.

What works is structural. Nothing cites to an authority that has not been pulled and read in the original. Nothing goes out over a signature without a named human having confirmed the parts that can be confirmed. The firm keeps a record of what was used where, so that the question can be answered later instead of reconstructed.
None of this is about distrusting the tool. It is the same discipline a firm applies to a first-year associate memo, which is also useful and also checked.

sections.heading: Build or buy, and the third option nobody names

paras.p: Buying is right when the problem is common, the product is mature, and the work it does is not where your firm differentiates. Research platforms and document review tools are usually in this category.

Building is right when the problem is yours specifically, the data is yours, and the value is in the arrangement rather than the model. A firm with twenty years of its own forms, its own matter history, and its own way of handling a recurring transaction can get more out of a modest system built around that material than out of an expensive general platform that knows nothing about it.

The third option is assembly, and it is where most small and mid-sized firms actually land. You are not building a model and you are not buying a monolith. You are connecting components you control, keeping your material on your own hardware where it needs to stay, and adding only the pieces that earn their place. It is less impressive on a slide and it is frequently the correct answer.
The question that decides it is not technical ambition. It is whether the thing you want is a commodity or is specific to how you practice.

sections.heading: Reading the product market without being sold to

paras.p: The category is loud and the claims are hard to compare because vendors describe different things with the same words.

A few questions cut through most of it. What does this replace, specifically, and what did that cost before. What does it do when it does not know, and can it tell you. Where does the output come from, and can a human follow it back to a source. What happens to our material if we leave in a year. Who is liable when it is wrong.
A product that cannot answer the fourth and fifth questions clearly is not ready for a firm that owes duties to clients, whatever it does in a demo.

sections.heading: Billing, disclosure, and the client relationship

paras.p: Fees must be reasonable under RPC 1.5, and that rule does the work here without needing an AI-specific gloss. A firm that completes in one hour what used to take four has to decide, deliberately, how that shows up on a bill, and the defensible answers are the ones the firm can explain out loud to the client it is billing.

On disclosure, the trend among sophisticated clients, particularly institutional ones, is to ask in the engagement letter and sometimes to restrict. Outside counsel guidelines increasingly address AI directly. A firm that has already decided its position answers that question in a sentence instead of scrambling.

sections.heading: Where firms actually get stuck

paras.p: Waiting for certainty. The rules are not going to resolve into a checklist before you have to act, and the firms doing this well made reasonable decisions early and revisited them.
Buying first and governing later, which produces a tool nobody is allowed to describe to a client.
Writing a policy that bans everything, which moves the use onto personal devices where it cannot be seen at all.
Treating it as an IT project. The decisions are professional responsibility decisions, and they belong to lawyers.

sections.heading: What I do in this area

paras.p: Three things, and they are separable.
Governance. Drafting the written policy, the intake and approval process for new tools, the verification workflow, and the client-facing language, sized to the firm rather than to a template.
Vendor and contract review. Reading the agreement that actually governs where your clients’ information goes, and telling you what it permits in the gaps rather than what the sales page says.

title: Alcohol Litigation and the Commerce Clause: Three Cases I Am Working On
titleTag: Alcohol Litigation and the Commerce Clause | Justin D. Leigh
description: How the dormant Commerce Clause reaches state liquor law, from Granholm to three current cases: brewery self-distribution in Oregon, distillery direct shipping in Washington, and a TTB challenge over vintage labels on cider and fruit wine.
lede: A brewery in Washington can sell a keg to a bar across the street. The same brewery, shipping that keg across a state line, runs into a wall of rules that exist for one reason: it is from somewhere else. For twenty years a small group of lawyers has been dismantling those rules one state at a time, and in the last few years I have been working on three of those cases.
intro: This piece is about why those rules keep losing, what the doctrine actually says, and where the three cases stand. It is written for people in the beverage industry who keep being told that something is simply not allowed.

sections.heading: The Twenty-first Amendment is narrower than people think

paras.p: Section 2 of the Twenty-first Amendment gives states authority over the transportation and importation of alcohol, and for decades it was treated as close to absolute. A state could regulate alcohol more or less however it liked, and the usual constitutional limits on protectionism were assumed not to apply.

The dormant Commerce Clause is the doctrine on the other side. It is the negative implication of Congress’s power to regulate interstate commerce: a state generally may not pass laws that discriminate against out-of-state businesses in order to protect its own. The question for alcohol was which of those two rules wins.

In 2005 the Supreme Court answered it in Granholm v. Heald. Michigan and New York let in-state wineries ship directly to consumers while barring out-of-state wineries from doing the same. The Court held that the Twenty-first Amendment restored to the states only the regulatory powers they held before Prohibition, and that those powers remain subject to the Commerce Clause. A state may regulate alcohol strictly, but it may not use that authority to favor its own producers. The decision was five to four.
Granholm is the hinge. Almost every case described below runs through it.

sections.heading: What happened after Granholm

paras.p: Granholm answered the question for wineries shipping to consumers. It did not answer it for retailers, for distilleries, for self-distribution, or for the dozens of other places where state alcohol codes draw an in-state versus out-of-state line. The Court returned to the subject in 2019 in Tennessee Wine and Spirits Retailers Association v. Thomas, striking down a durational residency requirement for retail liquor licenses and making clear that the nondiscrimination principle is not limited to producers.

The work of applying that principle, state by state and rule by rule, has largely fallen to a small number of lawyers who have been doing it since before Granholm. Robert Epstein and Alex Tanford, of Epstein Seif Porter and Beutel, brought many of the cases that produced Granholm and have continued the campaign across the country since. Their approach is incremental and deliberate: identify a state rule that treats an out-of-state business worse than an identical in-state one, find a plaintiff genuinely injured by it, and litigate the discrimination rather than the policy.
I have worked with them on two of the three cases below.

sections.heading: Garden Path and the Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission

paras.p: Oregon let in-state breweries sell their own beer directly to retailers. Out-of-state breweries had to go through a licensed wholesaler, which means giving up margin, giving up control of how the product is sold, and in practice often means not entering the market at all.
That is the Granholm pattern almost exactly, moved one step down the supply chain from consumers to retailers.

The case was brought on behalf of Garden Path Fermentation, a Washington producer. I facilitated the litigation and served as an expert witness. The state settled, and the result is that out-of-state breweries can now self-distribute in Oregon on the same terms as Oregon breweries.

Settlements do not make binding precedent, which is worth saying plainly. What they do is change the rule on the ground in that state and remove one more example of a regime that a later court would otherwise be told is normal and widespread.

sections.heading: Shady Knoll and direct shipping in Washington

paras.p: Washington permits direct-to-consumer shipping on terms that favor in-state operations. The Shady Knoll case was brought on behalf of out-of-state distilleries that want to ship directly to Washington consumers and cannot.

While summary judgment was under consideration, the Ninth Circuit decided Day v. Henry, an Arizona case. Arizona prevented retailers without in-state premises from shipping wine to Arizona consumers, and a divided panel upheld the scheme. The majority’s reasoning was that the law did not discriminate because an out-of-state retailer could establish an Arizona location and qualify for the same shipping privileges, and that out-of-state businesses had in fact done so.

That reasoning does not transfer to our case, and the reason is the distinction Granholm itself drew. Day was about retailers, and it turned on the availability of in-state licensure to an out-of-state retailer willing to open a physical location. Shady Knoll is about producers shipping their own product, which is the precise situation Granholm addressed. A rule that tells an out-of-state distillery it may ship only if it builds a presence in the state is not the same as a rule about retail licensing, and treating the two as interchangeable collapses a line the Supreme Court drew deliberately.
The trial court nonetheless applied Day to our case and granted summary judgment against us. We believe that was error, and it is the heart of the appeal. The appeal was argued over the summer.
The case is now deferred, and the reason it is deferred is the interesting part.

sections.heading: Why an ammunition case is holding up a liquor case

paras.p: The Ninth Circuit has deferred our case pending the en banc decision in Rhode v. Bonta. That case is not about alcohol at all. It is a challenge to California’s ammunition background check scheme, brought on Second Amendment grounds and on dormant Commerce Clause grounds.

The Commerce Clause half is what matters to us. The three-judge panel held that barring unlicensed out-of-state ammunition vendors from selling into California violated the dormant Commerce Clause. That is the same analytical move as our case, with a different product. The full court then took the case en banc, which wiped the panel decision, and it was argued and submitted in Pasadena in March 2026. As of this writing no en banc opinion has issued.

So the controlling statement of dormant Commerce Clause law in this circuit is, for the moment, unsettled, and a panel sensibly declined to decide our case before the full court decides what the test is. This is ordinary appellate practice and it is also why these cases take years.

It is also a useful illustration of something people in the beverage industry often miss: the doctrine that governs your shipping rules is not alcohol law. It is constitutional law that happens to be applied to alcohol, and it moves when a case about something else entirely moves.

sections.heading: Garden Path again, this time against the federal government

paras.p: The newest case is different in kind. It is not a Commerce Clause case and it is not against a state.

Federal regulations let a grape wine producer put the harvest year on the label. A producer of cider, mead, or fruit wine cannot, even where the statement is entirely accurate, because the vintage date rules are written around grapes. For a producer whose whole argument is that the fruit and the season matter, being forbidden to say which season is a real commercial injury.

The claim is that suppressing truthful, non-misleading commercial speech fails First Amendment scrutiny, and that the rule is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act. The defendant is the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau.

The procedural posture is where it sits now. The government moved to dismiss. We amended the complaint. The government has moved to dismiss again, and we are waiting on the trial court to decide whether the case goes forward at all. Nothing about the vintage rules themselves has been decided, and none of this is unusual in a case against a federal agency: the first real fight is usually about whether you are allowed to have the fight.

sections.heading: What the three have in common

paras.p: None of them argues that a state cannot regulate alcohol. That argument loses, and it should.

Each argues something narrower: that a particular rule treats an identical out-of-state business worse for no reason the state can actually defend, or that a federal rule forbids a true statement for no reason the agency can actually defend. The remedy sought is equal treatment rather than deregulation.
That is why these cases keep winning, and it is also why they proceed one rule at a time instead of in a single national stroke.

sections.heading: If you are in the industry

paras.p: The practical lesson is that "you are not allowed to do that" is sometimes a statement about a rule that has not been tested rather than a statement about the law. Three-tier structures, residency requirements, in-state presence requirements, and self-distribution rules all deserve a second look when they happen to fall only on businesses from somewhere else.

The threshold questions are mundane. Does the rule treat an in-state business and an out-of-state business differently. Is there a plaintiff who is genuinely injured by it rather than merely annoyed. Can the state articulate a reason that survives contact with the record. If the answers line up, there is a case. If they do not, there is not, and that is worth knowing early and cheaply.

I handle Washington liquor licensing and WSLCB compliance, formation and governance for breweries, wineries, cideries and distilleries, and constitutional and regulatory litigation of the kind described above. paras.p: The first conversation is short. What do you want to do, which rule stops you, and does that rule apply the same way to a competitor based in the state. That is usually enough to say whether there is something here.

title: Personal Injury Claims in Spokane: The Deadline, Your Own Insurance, and How Fault Gets Split
titleTag: Personal Injury Lawyer in Spokane, WA | Justin D. Leigh
description: How long you have to sue in Washington, why your own PIP and underinsured motorist coverage matter more than people expect, how fault gets split, and what a Spokane claim is really worth.
lede: The other driver ran the light on Division, the police report says so, and their insurer has already offered you two thousand dollars and a release. Your shoulder is worse at week six than it was at week one. Three things decide what happens next, and none of them is how obviously the other driver was at fault: the deadline, what coverage you bought for yourself before any of this happened, and how Washington splits fault when more than one person contributed.

sections.heading: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in Washington?

paras.p: Three years, in the ordinary case. RCW 4.16.080(2) sets a three-year limit on an action for "any other injury to the person or rights of another," and that is the provision that governs a car crash, a fall, a dog bite, and most other injury claims. The period runs from the injury.

Four things commonly change that number. If the person hurt was under eighteen when the claim accrued, RCW 4.16.190 excludes the time of that disability from the limitation period. If the defendant is a city, county, school district, or state agency, a tort claim has to be presented first and a sixty-day waiting period runs before suit, under RCW 4.96.020 and RCW 4.92.110. If the claim is against a health care provider, RCW 4.16.350 controls instead. That section runs three years from the act or omission, or one year from discovery if that is later, and in no event more than eight years. It also provides that a custodial parent's or guardian's knowledge is imputed to a claimant under eighteen, which means the tolling in RCW 4.16.190 does not apply to a child's medical negligence claim. And a wrongful death claim belongs to the personal representative of the estate, not to the family members directly, which takes a probate step before anything can be filed.

Three years sounds like plenty and behaves like less. Evidence has a shorter life than the deadline: vehicles are repaired or crushed, intersection video is overwritten in days, the store resurfaces the floor, and a witness who was happy to talk at the scene has moved twice.

sections.heading: Your own insurance pays first, and that is not a favor

paras.p: The at-fault driver's insurer will not pay your medical bills as you go. It pays once, at the end, in exchange for a release. That leaves a gap of months or years, and the coverage designed to fill it is on your own policy.

Personal injury protection, almost always called PIP, pays your medical expenses regardless of who caused the crash, up to the limits you bought and for treatment that is reasonable and related to the crash. RCW 48.22.085 requires every new or renewed automobile liability policy in Washington to offer PIP as an optional coverage. A named insured may reject it, but only in writing, and the statute makes that rejection binding as to all levels of coverage and on everyone who would otherwise have been insured. If you cannot remember rejecting it, pull the declarations page rather than guessing.

Using your own PIP is not making a claim against yourself and it is not an admission. It keeps you in treatment, which is both the medical point and, bluntly, the evidentiary one: a gap in treatment is the first thing an adjuster will point at when arguing that you recovered early.

sections.heading: Underinsured motorist coverage is the claim people forget

paras.p: The driver who hit you may carry the state minimum, or nothing at all, or may have a policy that three people are already claiming against. Underinsured motorist coverage, which in Washington also covers the uninsured driver and the hit-and-run, is the coverage that answers that. It is on your own policy and it is the reason two identical crashes end differently.

RCW 48.22.030(2) does more than require an offer. No new or renewed automobile liability policy may be issued on a vehicle registered or principally garaged in Washington unless this coverage is in it, subject to the exceptions written into the same subsection, which include a motorcycle or motor-driven cycle and a vehicle owned or regularly available to you or a family member that is not insured under the policy's liability coverage. RCW 48.22.030(3) sets the amount for bodily injury: the same as your own third party liability limits, unless you rejected it. Rejection takes a writing from a named insured or spouse under RCW 48.22.030(4). RCW 48.22.030(1) defines an underinsured motor vehicle to include one with no applicable liability coverage at all and one whose total applicable limits come to less than the damages you are legally entitled to recover, and subsection (2) extends the same protection to hit-and-run and phantom vehicles.

Two practical points. The amount of underinsured motorist coverage you carry is the real ceiling on a serious claim against a minimally insured driver, and raising it is usually inexpensive. And settling with the at-fault driver's insurer without first dealing with your own underinsured motorist carrier can destroy the claim against your own policy, which is one of the reasons the early release is worth reading slowly.

sections.heading: How Washington splits fault, and why splitting it does not end your claim

paras.p: Washington is a pure comparative fault state. RCW 4.22.005 provides that contributory fault chargeable to the claimant "diminishes proportionately the amount awarded as compensatory damages," and then says the thing that matters most: it "does not bar recovery." Being partly at fault reduces the number. It does not end the case, and there is no threshold at which it does.

Fault is defined broadly. RCW 4.22.015 includes negligent and reckless acts and omissions, strict liability, product liability, breach of warranty, unreasonable assumption of risk, and the "unreasonable failure to avoid an injury or to mitigate damages." That last phrase is why not following medical advice can show up as a percentage against you.

When several parties are at fault, RCW 4.22.070(1) has the trier of fact assign a percentage to every entity that caused the damages, including the claimant, and liability is several only rather than joint. There are two exceptions, and the second is the one nobody expects: under RCW 4.22.070(1)(b), if the trier of fact finds the claimant was not at fault, the defendants against whom judgment is entered are jointly and severally liable for the sum of their proportionate shares. In a multi-defendant case where one defendant cannot pay, a finding of zero fault on your part is worth a great deal more than it sounds.

sections.heading: How much is my car accident case worth?

paras.p: There is no formula and no multiplier, and anybody quoting one is selling something. Washington damages in an injury case divide into economic losses, which are the medical bills and the lost earnings and the things with receipts, and noneconomic losses, which are pain, loss of function, and the parts of a life that changed. Both are proved, not calculated.

The economic side is won with documents: complete records, a treating provider willing to state what is permanent, wage records rather than estimates, and a plan for future care that somebody qualified has actually priced. The noneconomic side is won with specifics. Not that you are in pain, but that you cannot lift your youngest, that you stopped the thing you did every Saturday, that you sleep on the couch now.

The timing point follows from that. A claim valued before treatment is complete is valued without knowing what the injury is, which is why the fast early offer is nearly always the cheap one. It arrives at the moment the insurer knows the least and you need the money the most, and that is not a coincidence.

sections.heading: When someone dies: wrongful death and survival claims

paras.p: Two different claims, and both run through the estate rather than the family. RCW 4.20.010 gives the personal representative the right to sue for the economic and noneconomic damages the statutory beneficiaries suffered as a result of the death. RCW 4.20.020 lists those beneficiaries: the spouse or state registered domestic partner and the children, including stepchildren, and if there are none of those, the parents or siblings.

Alongside that, the survival statutes carry forward what the person who died could have brought. RCW 4.20.046 lets the personal representative recover the estate's economic losses and, for the beneficiaries named in RCW 4.20.020, noneconomic damages for the pain, anxiety, emotional distress, or humiliation that the decedent personally suffered. Both of those pieces turn on there being a beneficiary the statute names. RCW 4.20.060 keeps a personal injury action alive where the injury occasioned the death, and it too is conditioned on a surviving spouse, state registered domestic partner, or child, or failing those a parent or sibling.

The 2019 amendments to these sections widened who can recover, and the legislature made them expressly remedial and retroactive to all claims not already time barred. The practical first step is still administrative rather than legal: somebody has to be appointed personal representative before any of these claims can be filed at all.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The recorded statement to the other side's adjuster, given early, while you are still describing the injury as sore.
A signed release in exchange for a small check, which ends every claim including the ones nobody has valued yet.
A gap in treatment. Whatever the reason, it reads in the file as recovery.
Nobody ever looks at the claimant's own declarations page, so PIP goes unused and underinsured motorist coverage goes unclaimed.
Social media. A photograph of you at a wedding, holding a drink and smiling, becomes an exhibit about your limitations.
Waiting. Not past the deadline, just long enough that the vehicle is gone, the video is overwritten, and the scene has been repaired.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: Reading every policy in the case, yours included, because the coverage usually decides the ceiling. Preserving evidence that has a shorter life than the claim. Keeping you off the phone with the adjuster. Making sure the treating records say what is actually wrong with you. Running every deadline separately when a government entity or a health care provider is involved. And giving you a straight answer about comparative fault early, because a realistic number now is worth more than an optimistic one later.

I handle personal injury and wrongful death claims from my office in downtown Spokane, and I represent clients throughout Washington. I am admitted in Washington, WSBA #55307, and Oregon, OSB #242384.

If you were hurt and are not sure what to do next, I offer a free consultation by appointment at my Spokane office, 601 W. 1st Ave., Suite 1400. Bring the police report or incident number, your own insurance declarations page, and anything the other insurer has already sent you.

title: Dog Bites in Washington: When You Can Sue, and the One Defense That Beats It
titleTag: Dog Bite Lawyer in Spokane, WA | Justin D. Leigh
description: Washington lets you sue a dog owner for a bite without proving the dog was vicious before. When you can sue, the provocation defense, who actually pays, and the three-year deadline.
lede: A dog you have walked past a hundred times came off a porch and took hold of your daughter's face. You are in an urgent care waiting room, somebody has handed you a phone number for animal control, and that evening a claims adjuster for the owner's insurance company calls and is very pleasant. Washington's dog bite statute is unusually favorable to the person who was bitten. The single question that decides most of these cases is one you may already have answered out loud to that adjuster.

sections.heading: Washington has no one bite rule

paras.p: In many states you have to prove the owner knew the dog was dangerous, which usually means proving it had bitten somebody before. Washington does not work that way. RCW 16.08.040(1) makes the owner of a dog that bites a person liable for the damages the bitten person suffers, and then adds the clause that matters: "regardless of the former viciousness of such dog or the owner's knowledge of such viciousness."

A dog with a spotless history, a dog that has never growled at anyone, an owner who is genuinely shocked. None of that is a defense to a bite. Liability is strict, which moves the fight off whether the owner did anything wrong and onto two different questions: were you lawfully where you were standing, and did you provoke the dog.

There is one carve-out in the statute itself. RCW 16.08.040(2) says the section does not apply to the lawful application of a police dog. A police dog deployment is a different case, usually an excessive force claim under the Fourth Amendment rather than a dog bite claim, and it runs on different rules and different deadlines.

sections.heading: Where you were standing when it happened

paras.p: The statute covers a bite in a public place, and a bite on private property if you were lawfully there, including on the dog owner's own property. A delivery driver on the walkway, a guest in the kitchen, a child in a front yard she was invited into: all lawfully present.

RCW 16.08.050 defines lawful presence as being on the property "with the express or implied consent of the owner," and then attaches a proviso that does real work: consent "shall not be presumed when the property of the owner is fenced or reasonably posted." A fence or a sign does not end the claim. It removes the assumption that you were welcome and puts you to proving you were invited.

So the first thing worth writing down is the geography. Which side of the fence you were on, whether the gate was open, whether there was a sign and what it actually said, whether you had been there before and at whose invitation. Photograph the fence line and the sign the same week, because both change.

sections.heading: Provocation is a complete defense, and that is what the adjuster is asking about

paras.p: RCW 16.08.060 is a single sentence: "Proof of provocation of the attack by the injured person shall be a complete defense to an action for damages." Complete, not partial. Provocation does not reduce the claim the way ordinary comparative fault does. It ends it.

That is why the friendly early phone call matters so much. Was she playing with him. Did she grab his tail. Had she been teasing him through the fence before. Those are not small talk. A recorded answer given on day one by a frightened parent, or by a seven-year-old, gets read back a year later in a deposition.

What counts as provocation is a question of fact, and with young children it is heavily contested, because a child doing what children do around animals is not the same thing as a person tormenting a dog. Say what happened accurately and stop there. Nothing obliges you to give a recorded statement to the dog owner's insurer. A policy you bought yourself is different, because it usually carries a duty to cooperate.

sections.heading: A bite is not the only way a dog hurts someone, and the statute only covers bites

paras.p: RCW 16.08.040 is built around the word bite. A great deal of real dog injury is not a bite. A large dog that jumps up and knocks an older person onto a sidewalk. A dog that bolts into the road and causes a collision. A dog that attacks another dog, with the owner hurt trying to pull them apart. A dog that chases a cyclist into a ditch.

Those are ordinary negligence claims, and they are harder, because negligence puts the owner's knowledge back in issue: what the owner knew or should have known about this particular dog, whether the restraint was adequate, whether a local leash ordinance was broken. Washington recognizes both routes, and a careful claim often pleads the statute and negligence together, so that an argument about whether teeth actually broke skin does not end everything.

Injury to another dog is handled as damage to property plus veterinary cost, which lands badly on people who think of a dog as family. It is better to know that going in than to find it out from an adjuster.

sections.heading: Dog attack laws in Washington: dangerous dog and potentially dangerous dog

paras.p: RCW 16.08.070 defines a potentially dangerous dog as one that, unprovoked, bites a person or a domestic animal, or chases or approaches a person in public "in a menacing fashion or apparent attitude of attack." A dangerous dog is one that inflicts severe injury on a person without provocation, kills a domestic animal off the owner's property, or bites again after already having been found potentially dangerous with notice to the owner. Severe injury has a hard definition in the same section: "broken bones or disfiguring lacerations requiring multiple sutures or cosmetic surgery."

Those designations drive restraint and criminal exposure rather than your damages. RCW 16.08.090(1) makes it unlawful for the owner of a dangerous dog to let it outside its proper enclosure unless it is muzzled and held on a substantial chain or leash by a responsible person, and RCW 16.08.100 provides for confiscation, destruction in some circumstances, and criminal penalties reaching a class C felony. RCW 16.08.090(3) also lists who cannot trigger a dangerous dog declaration at all, including a person committing a willful trespass or another tort on the owner's premises, a person tormenting or abusing the dog, and a person committing a crime.

The reason this still matters to a civil claim is evidence. An animal control file can hold a prior potentially dangerous designation, a neighbor's complaint from two years ago, or an earlier bite report, and all of it bears on the negligence theory and on what a jury thinks the owner should have known. Request the file early. Agencies purge records and witnesses move.

sections.heading: Can I sue my neighbor for a dog bite, and who actually pays?

paras.p: The defendant is the owner. RCW 16.08.070(7) defines owner broadly, reaching any person or entity "possessing, harboring, keeping, having an interest in, or having control or custody of" the animal, but that definition applies by its own terms only to RCW 16.08.070 through 16.08.100, the dangerous dog sections. RCW 16.08.040 does not carry its own definition, so whether a person who was keeping the dog but did not own it is liable for the bite is a question to sort out early rather than assume.

In practice the money is homeowner's or renter's liability insurance, and the insurer both defends the owner and writes the check. Two things are worth checking before anybody assumes there is coverage. Some policies exclude particular breeds or exclude animal liability outright, and the owner often does not know that. And a landlord is not automatically on the hook for a tenant's dog, which takes showing the landlord knew about this dog's dangerous propensity and had some control over whether it stayed.

If the dog belongs to a city, a county, a school district, or the state, a separate statute controls what you have to do before you can sue at all, and missing that step ends a strong case. That is covered in the article on claims against government entities.

sections.heading: How long you have to bring a dog bite claim in Washington

paras.p: Three years. A personal injury claim runs under RCW 4.16.080(2), which sets a three-year limit for "any other injury to the person or rights of another," and the clock starts at the injury.

For a child the clock runs differently. RCW 4.16.190 excludes from the limitation period the time a claimant was under eighteen, so a five-year-old's claim is not gone at eight. That is not a reason to wait. Scars mature and change, witnesses move away, the dog is rehomed or euthanized, and photographs taken in the first week are worth more than any later description of what the wound looked like.
Three years is the outer boundary, not the plan. Nobody can value an injury before treatment is far enough along to know what the permanent part of it is.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The recorded statement given on day one, before anybody has slept, which locks in a version of events that a careful account would have stated differently.
No photographs of the wound before it closed, and none of the property. A healed scar photographs as a thin line. The same injury at seventy-two hours does not.
Medical records that never use the word dog. Urgent care charts a laceration, the follow-up charts a wound check, and eighteen months later there is no document tying the injury to the animal.

Treating the owner as the adversary. The adversary is the insurer. The owner is frequently a neighbor you still have to live beside, and the claim is against a policy they pay for precisely so this can be handled without a feud.

Taking the first offer before a plastic surgery consult. Scarring is the category most often undervalued, and scarring on a child's face is frequently permanent. A consult that prices revision surgery over the years ahead is what puts the future cost of the injury into the claim instead of leaving it out.
Assuming a fence or a sign ends it. Under RCW 16.08.050 it changes what has to be proved. It does not decide the case.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: Most of the work is early and unglamorous. Getting the animal control and law enforcement file before it ages. Finding the policy and reading its exclusions. Documenting the scene and the wound while both still show what happened. Keeping you off the phone with the adjuster. Getting the right treating specialist to say, in writing, what this injury will mean in ten years. Somebody also has to tell you honestly when provocation is a real problem in your case instead of a bluff, because that answer changes what the claim is worth.

title: Suing the City, the County, or a School District in Washington: The Claim You Have to File First
titleTag: Suing a City or County, Spokane WA | Justin D. Leigh
description: Before you can sue a Washington city, county, school district or state agency, you have to present a tort claim and wait sixty days. What the form requires and how the tolling works.
lede: A city bus changed lanes into the side of your car. A county road crew left a trench open overnight. Your son broke his arm on a school playground that had been reported twice. A state patrol cruiser rear-ended you at a light. In each of those, you have a claim against a government, and in each of those Washington puts a step in front of the courthouse door that has nothing to do with whether you are right. Miss the step and the case is over.

sections.heading: Washington governments are liable, and that is the starting point

paras.p: Washington gave up most of its immunity from tort suits decades ago, and for local government the statute says so plainly. RCW 4.96.010(1) makes all local governmental entities liable for damages arising out of their own tortious conduct, or that of their officers, employees, and volunteers acting in their official duties, "to the same extent as if they were a private person or corporation." Whether the entity was acting in a governmental or a proprietary capacity does not matter.

The same section then attaches the condition that catches people: "Filing a claim for damages within the time allowed by law shall be a condition precedent to the commencement of any action claiming damages." A condition precedent is not a formality. It is a thing that has to have happened before a lawsuit can exist.

RCW 4.96.010(2) defines local governmental entity broadly: a county, a city, a town, a special district, a municipal or quasi-municipal corporation, a joint municipal utility services authority, an entity created by interlocal agreement, or a public hospital. That sweeps in school districts, fire districts, transit authorities, ports, public utility districts, and hospital districts.

sections.heading: Can I sue the city, the county, or a school district?

paras.p: A claim against a local entity is presented to an agent the governing body has appointed to receive claims. RCW 4.96.020(2) requires that agent's identity and business address to be a public record and to be recorded with the auditor of the county where the entity sits, which is how you find out where to send it. A claim is presented when the form is delivered in person or received by that agent by regular, registered, or certified mail with return receipt requested.

paras.sub: The state and its agencies: chapter 4.92 RCW

paras.p: A claim against the state, a state officer, or a state employee goes to the Office of Risk Management. RCW 4.92.100(1) allows delivery in person, by regular, registered, or certified mail with return receipt requested, by fax, or as an email attachment, and it sets out what an electronic signature has to carry with it. This is the route for the Department of Transportation, the Department of Corrections, the State Patrol, the state universities, and the rest of state government.

Getting the wrong statute is a live risk, because the entity that hurt you is not always the one whose name is on the vehicle or the building. A road can be city, county, or state within a few blocks. A transit bus belongs to a transit authority, not to the city. A public hospital may be a district, and a private hospital is neither.

sections.heading: What presenting a claim actually requires

paras.p: For claims presented after July 26, 2009, claims go on the standard tort claim form maintained by the Office of Risk Management in the Department of Enterprise Services, which the statute requires to be posted on that agency's website. A local entity must make the standard form available and may also offer its own, and presenting either one satisfies the chapter.

RCW 4.96.020(3)(a) and RCW 4.92.100(1)(a) set the same minimum contents: your name, date of birth, and contact information; a description of the conduct and the circumstances that brought about the injury; a description of the injury or damage; the time and place it happened; the names and contact information of everyone involved, if known; the amount of damages claimed; and your actual residence both when the claim arose and when you present it.

Signature matters more than people expect. The form must be signed by the claimant verifying the claim, or by an attorney-in-fact under a written power of attorney, or by an attorney admitted to practice in Washington on the claimant's behalf, or by a court-approved guardian or guardian ad litem. A claim signed by the wrong person is a defect worth arguing about, and it is entirely avoidable.
One detail that relieves a common worry: the amount of damages you write on the form is not admissible at trial. It is required, and it is not a cap or an admission.

sections.heading: The sixty days, the tolling, and the five court days

paras.p: After the claim is presented you have to wait. RCW 4.96.020(4) bars commencing the action against a local entity "until sixty calendar days have elapsed" after the claim was first presented, and RCW 4.92.110 says the same for the state.

Both sections then protect the deadline rather than punishing you for the wait. The applicable limitation period is tolled during the sixty days, so the waiting period does not eat three months of your three years. And for purposes of the limitation period, an action commenced within five court days after the sixty calendar days have elapsed is deemed to have been presented on the first day after that period ended, which is a small grace built in for the filing itself.

In practice that means the arithmetic has to be done on paper, not in your head. The date the agent received the claim is the date everything else is counted from, and the sixty days and the tolled stretch of the limitation period both have to be calculated before a complaint is filed.

sections.heading: Substantial compliance, and what it does not forgive

paras.p: Both chapters are generous about how a claim is written. RCW 4.96.020(5) says that as to content and all procedural requirements, the section "must be liberally construed so that substantial compliance will be deemed satisfactory," and RCW 4.92.100(3) says the same for state claims. Imperfect wording and a missing detail are usually survivable.

What liberal construction does not supply is a claim that was never presented, or one presented after the limitation period ran. The rule is forgiving about the contents of the document and unforgiving about its existence and its timing.

The statute also disciplines the government. RCW 4.96.020(2) says that a local entity's own failure to comply with the section "precludes that local governmental entity from raising a defense under this chapter," and RCW 4.96.020(3)(d) waives the related defense when the entity's own form fails to ask for required information or lists the wrong agent. An entity's form may not demand your Social Security number, and while it may ask for extra information, it cannot deny the claim because you left the extra blank.

sections.heading: Section 1983 claims do not go through this

paras.p: If the claim is a federal civil rights claim under 42 U.S.C. section 1983, the state claim filing statute does not apply to it. In Felder v. Casey, 487 U.S. 131 (1988), the Supreme Court held Wisconsin's notice-of-claim statute preempted as inconsistent with federal law when applied to section 1983 actions brought in state court.

The practical consequence is that a single incident can carry two claims on two tracks. An arrest that broke your wrist might support a state law negligence or assault claim, which needs a presented claim and a sixty-day wait, alongside a Fourth Amendment excessive force claim under section 1983, which does not. Dropping the state claim filing step because the federal claim does not need it is a way to lose half a case.

Picking which claims to bring, and in which court, is its own decision with consequences for immunity, fees, and the jury pool. The companion article on section 1983 claims in Washington covers that side of it.

sections.heading: The three years underneath all of it

paras.p: The claim filing statute is a gate, not a limitation period. The limitation period is still three years for a personal injury claim, under RCW 4.16.080(2), and RCW 4.96.020(2) requires the claim to be presented to the agent "within the applicable period of limitations within which an action must be commenced."

Read together that produces a deadline earlier than three years in every practical sense. A claim presented on the last day of the third year is timely as a claim, but the sixty-day wait means the lawsuit cannot be filed on time without relying on the tolling provision to carry it. That provision exists and it works. Relying on it with no margin is still a bad plan.

Where a child is hurt, RCW 4.16.190 excludes the time the claimant was under eighteen from the limitation period, which also affects the claim presentment window because that window is defined by the limitation period. One exception matters here, because a public hospital district is both a local governmental entity under this chapter and a health care provider: RCW 4.16.350 imputes a custodial parent's knowledge to a claimant under eighteen and says so notwithstanding RCW 4.16.190, so a child's claim for medical negligence does not get that tolling. That interaction is worth getting advice on rather than assuming either way.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The claim goes to the receptionist, or to the risk pool, or to the insurer, instead of to the agent recorded with the county auditor. Delivery to the right person is part of what presentment means.
The wrong entity gets the claim. A claim presented to a city for a crash on a state highway, or to a county for an injury on transit property, is not a claim against the entity that is liable.
Nobody notes the date of receipt. Return receipt requested exists for exactly this reason, and the sixty days cannot be counted without it.
The complaint is filed on day forty. Early filing is a dismissal risk, and the cure is not always a refiling, because by then the limitation period may have moved.

Public records that would prove notice are never requested. A prior complaint about the same intersection, the same stair, or the same playground is often the difference between an accident and a claim, and the Public Records Act is the way to get it.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: The early work is identifying the correct entity and the correct statute, finding the recorded agent, presenting a claim that is complete and properly signed, calendaring the sixty days and the limitation period together, and pulling the agency's own records about the condition or the employee before anybody is on notice to be careful with them. Someone also has to read the immunity doctrines honestly, because discretionary acts, public duty, and the particulars of road design each carry real defenses that are better understood before a claim than after.

I am admitted in Washington, WSBA #55307, and Oregon, OSB #242384. I represent clients throughout Washington.

If a government entity injured you or someone in your family, I offer a free consultation by appointment at my Spokane office, 601 W. 1st Ave., Suite 1400. Bring the date it happened, any incident or report number you were given, and the name of the agency as it appeared on the vehicle, the uniform, or the sign.
