title: An LCB Violation Notice in Washington: Twenty Days, Three Options, and What the Penalty Will Be
titleTag: LCB Violation Notice in Washington, Penalties | Justin D. Leigh
practiceArea: Alcohol Beverage Licensing and Regulatory Compliance
description: An administrative violation notice from the Liquor and Cannabis Board starts a twenty-day clock, and letting it run is itself an answer. What the three options mean, what the penalty will be, and when the Board does not wait.
lede: You opened the mail and there is an administrative violation notice from the Liquor and Cannabis Board, with a recommended penalty printed on it. Or you are eighteen weeks into an application for a taproom and the city has filed something. Both of those run on clocks that are shorter than they look, and in the second one the clock that matters is not yours. The licensee who does nothing for three weeks has not delayed a decision. He has made one.

sections.heading: Who the Liquor and Cannabis Board is, and what it can do to your license

paras.p: The Board licenses and regulates every business in Washington that makes, moves or sells alcohol: breweries, wineries, distilleries, distributors, bars, restaurants, taprooms, grocers and the special occasion licensee running a one-night event. The licensing side lives in chapter 66.24 RCW and the penalty side in chapter 314-29 WAC, and the two are worth reading as one thing, because the decisions you make at application are the ones the enforcement division measures you against later.

When the Board moves against a license, that is not an informal agency decision. RCW 66.08.150 makes any denial of reissuance, and any revocation, suspension or modification of a license, an adjudicative proceeding under the Administrative Procedure Act, chapter 34.05 RCW. An opportunity for a hearing must be given before a revocation or a modification, and before a suspension except in the emergency case described further down.

That same statute contains the sentence that catches people. RCW 66.08.150(3): "No hearing may be required until demanded by the applicant, permittee, or licensee." The right exists. It does not arrive on its own.

sections.heading: How long does it take to get a liquor license in Washington, and what actually holds it up

paras.p: Nobody can give you a date, and anyone who does is guessing. What can be described is the sequence, because almost every delay comes from one of three places in it.

RCW 66.24.010(2) lets the Board inspect the premises and inquire into all matters in connection with the construction and operation of the premises, and it lets the Board consider an applicant's prior criminal conduct, their administrative violation history with the Board, and a criminal history record check. Where that check goes to the FBI, the Board must require fingerprinting. This is worth building into the schedule rather than assuming away in a lease.

The Board notifies the chief executive officer of the city or town, or the county legislative authority where the premises are outside a city or town. Under RCW 66.24.010(8)(c) that authority then has twenty days from the date the notice was transmitted to file written objections against the applicant or the premises, and for a renewal the window runs to at least thirty days before expiry. The Board may extend it.

Those objections are not a formality. RCW 66.24.010(12) requires the Board to give substantial weight to a local objection based on chronic illegal activity, which the statute defines as a pervasive pattern of activity threatening public health, safety and welfare, documented in things like police reports, calls for service and emergency medical response data, or alternatively an unreasonably high number of DUI citations under RCW 46.61.502 tied to the applicant's operation of a licensed premises. A jurisdiction with a file on your block can make that file your problem.

RCW 66.24.010(9)(a) requires written notice of the application, with receipt verification, to churches and schools within five hundred feet of the premises to be licensed, and to the public institutions in that radius that the Board has identified as appropriate to receive notice. The measurement is along the most direct route over public walks and streets from the school's main entrance to the nearest public entrance of your premises, not as the crow flies. For premises not already licensed, the Board may not issue the license if the premises are within five hundred feet of a tax-supported public elementary or secondary school and an official representative of that school objects in writing, on proximity grounds, within twenty days of receiving the notice. The Board may extend that objection period, and under RCW 66.24.010(10) the restriction does not bar the assumption of an existing license or the relocation of licensed premises inside the restricted area.

Private schools are treated differently and are worth knowing about before you sign anything. Under RCW 66.24.010(9)(c) the Board must fully consider and give substantial weight to a private school's objection, and where it issues the license anyway it has to write to the school explaining why.

sections.heading: The administrative violation notice, and the twenty days that follow

paras.p: WAC 314-29-005 says what the notice contains: a short narrative of what the officer is charging, the dates, a copy of the law or rule allegedly violated, an outline of your options, and the recommended penalty.

WAC 314-29-010(1) gives you twenty days from receipt to do one of three things, on a form the agency provides. Accept the recommended penalty. Request a settlement conference in writing. Request an administrative hearing in writing.
Twenty days from RECEIPT, not from the postmark and not from the day you got round to opening it. Write the date on the envelope.

What happens if you let it pass is set out in the same rule and it is worse than most owners expect. The recommended suspension goes into effect. If the violation included a monetary penalty, then after day twenty and up to thirty days from the DATE OF THE NOTICE, which is a different starting point from the twenty days to respond, you can still pay the recommended penalty plus a twenty-five percent fee instead of serving the suspension. If the penalty was money rather than suspension, you owe that plus a twenty-five percent late fee, due within thirty days of the notice date. On a failure to pay, collection provisions take effect immediately, or the Board may institute other action it considers appropriate, including revocation. An unpaid debt can also be assigned to a collection agency, after the Board has attempted to advise the licensee of the debt and at least thirty days have passed.

Two further consequences sit at the end of that rule and they are the ones that end businesses. A licensee who has failed to respond to a violation notice, or who has outstanding fines, is not eligible to renew the license. And failing to address monetary penalties on two or more violation notices within a two-year period results in cancellation.

sections.heading: What the three options actually mean

paras.p: Fast, and final, and it goes on your record. That record is what the next notice gets measured against, which is why accepting a first violation without reading the penalty tables is a decision about your second violation as much as your first.

A conversation with a hearing examiner or an enforcement captain about the circumstances of the charge, the recommended penalty and any aggravating or mitigating factors, rather than a trial about the facts. It is where mitigation gets heard. Any compromise reached there is not self-executing: it goes to the Board for approval, and if the Board does not approve it you can renegotiate, accept the original penalty, or request a hearing. WAC 314-29-015(4) lets the Board impose a different penalty than the standard one based on mitigating or aggravating circumstances, and lets it offer a monetary option in lieu of suspension days on mitigation. The rule gives two examples of mitigation that may mean fewer suspension days or a lower monetary option: a signed acknowledgment of the business's alcohol policy on file for each employee, and an employee training plan that includes annual training on liquor laws. The Board also keeps a public list of business practices as further examples, and neither list is exclusive. If you have those, bring them. If you do not, that sentence is a to-do list.

A contested proceeding under the Administrative Procedure Act, usually before an administrative law judge appointed at the Board's request under RCW 66.24.010(3)(d) and chapter 34.12 RCW, with an initial order that can be reviewed. An initial order that nobody seeks review of becomes the final order.

sections.heading: What the penalty will be, and why the second one costs so much more

paras.p: WAC 314-29-015 sorts violations into five groups: public safety, regulatory, licensing, nonretail violations involving manufacture supply and distribution, and public safety at sports entertainment facilities. The schedules are guidelines rather than a tariff, and the Board can depart from them in either direction.

The arithmetic that matters is the window. For chapter 314-29 WAC purposes a two-year window is measured from the date one violation occurred to the date a later one occurred. Not from when the notice issued, not from when you paid.

Group One, the public safety violations, is counted in a way that surprises people. WAC 314-29-020(2) says Group 1 violations are counted sequentially rather than independently, so a later violation of a different type inside the same group still counts as the next offense. The rule's own example: over service one day and a sale to a minor a week later makes the sale to a minor a SECOND offense, because both sit in the same group. And beyond a first Group One violation, the notice does not carry a monetary option at all. The Board may still offer one at a settlement conference on mitigation, which is a reason to request the conference rather than write a check.
That is the whole economics of a first violation. Treating it as a parking ticket is what makes the second one a suspension you cannot buy your way out of.

sections.heading: The violations that cancel a license on the first offense

paras.p: Most of the schedules escalate. A few do not. Under WAC 314-29-030, which covers licensing violations, several entries read cancellation of license in the first-violation column with nothing before it.
A true party of interest violation under RCW 66.24.010(1) and WAC 314-12-030 is one of them. So is failure to furnish required documents, and misrepresentation of fact.

True party of interest is the one worth stopping on. RCW 66.24.010(1) and WAC 314-12-030(1) require the license to be issued in the name of the true party or parties in interest, and RCW 66.24.010(13)(c) lets the Board require lease agreements, operating agreements and other contracts to satisfy itself that the licensee really retains ownership and control of the premises. Who counts turns on the specific arrangement, which is why a structure that feels like ordinary business is worth checking before the Board checks it. The schedule for getting it wrong has one column.

sections.heading: Summary suspension, when the Board does not wait

paras.p: RCW 66.08.150(4) lets the Board suspend a license for up to one hundred eighty days with no prior hearing where it finds that public health, safety or welfare imperatively require emergency action, and it must put that finding in the order. Proceedings for revocation or other action have to be promptly instituted and determined, and an administrative law judge may extend the summary suspension period for up to one calendar year if the main proceeding cannot finish in the first one hundred eighty days because of the licensee's own actions.

The statute does require the enforcement division to complete a preliminary staff investigation before asking the Board for an emergency suspension. If this happens to you, that sentence is the first thing to ask about.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The notice sits on the office desk for three weeks because the owner is waiting to talk to somebody. Day twenty-one is not a late start. It is a decision already made.
A first violation gets paid off to make it go away, with nobody reading what it does to the second one inside the two-year window.
The monetary option is treated as the cheap route when the settlement conference was the route that could have reduced the underlying penalty.

Nobody has the mitigation the rule actually names. Signed alcohol policy acknowledgments and an annual training plan are cheap to put in place before a violation, and a plan written after the notice arrives does not show the history the rule is looking for.
The applicant never finds out the city filed an objection, because the twenty days ran against the local authority and nobody was watching that calendar.
An ownership change, a new investor, or a management agreement goes through without anyone asking whether it moved the true party of interest. That is the one with cancellation in the first column.
Renewal is treated as administrative while a fine is outstanding, and the licensee discovers at renewal that they were not eligible.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: Most of the value is in the first week. Working out which group the charge sits in and what it does to the next two years, rather than only what it costs today. Choosing between the settlement conference and the hearing on something other than instinct. Assembling the mitigation the rule names before the conference instead of describing it afterwards. Getting the demand for a hearing in writing and on time, because the right exists only once it is demanded. On the licensing side, it is finding the objection before it hardens, and reading an ownership structure for true party of interest exposure before the Board reads it.

I handle Washington liquor licensing and LCB enforcement work from my office in downtown Spokane, and I have appeared in administrative proceedings before the Board. The work covers breweries, wineries, bars, restaurants and taprooms. I am admitted in Washington, WSBA #55307, and Oregon, OSB #242384. I represent clients throughout Washington.

If a violation notice has arrived, the date you received it is the first thing to establish and the twenty days are already running. I offer a free consultation by appointment at my Spokane office, 601 W. 1st Ave., Suite 1400. Bring the notice itself, the envelope, and whatever you have in the way of training records and written policies.

title: What Washington's rent increase cap actually says
titleTag: Spokane Landlord-Tenant Lawyer, Rent Caps | Justin D. Leigh
description: Washington caps residential rent increases under RCW 59.18.700 and requires cause to end most tenancies. The deposit and lockout sections shift attorneys' fees. A Spokane attorney on what the statute says, for landlords and for tenants.
lede: Washington caps how much a landlord can raise the rent, and the cap is newer than a lot of the leases still in circulation. I represent landlords and tenants, and the same two misreadings arrive from both directions: owners who think the cap is a flat percentage they can look up once, and renters who think an over-cap increase is something they can simply refuse to pay. Neither is right.
intro: The cap sits inside chapter 59.18 RCW, the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act, which already governed most of what the two sides actually fight about. Reading the new rent sections without the rest of the chapter is how an owner ends up right on the percentage and defective on the notice.

sections.heading: Can my landlord raise my rent?

paras.p: Yes, within limits, and the first limit is timing, not amount. Under RCW 59.18.700(1)(a)(i) a landlord may not increase the rent during the first 12 months after the tenancy begins, whatever the lease type, and the only way around that is an exemption under RCW 59.18.710. After the first year, the ceiling for any 12-month period is seven percent plus the consumer price index, or 10 percent, whichever of the two is less.

I am deliberately not printing a percentage here. RCW 59.18.700(1)(c) ties the index to the June 12-month percent change in the consumer price index for the Seattle area, and has the Department of Commerce calculate and publish the maximum increase for the following calendar year each year. An owner who builds a notice on last year's number has used the wrong figure, and where last year's number is the higher one, the increase is over the cap.

RCW 59.18.700(1)(b) then provides that the cap does not prohibit adjusting the rent by any amount once the tenant has vacated and the tenancy has ended, so the limit travels with the tenancy rather than the unit. These rent provisions also expire July 1, 2040.

sections.heading: How much notice to raise rent in Washington?

paras.p: The day count is in RCW 59.18.140, not in an old form packet. Subsection (3)(a) requires a minimum of 90 days' prior written notice of a rent increase, and no increase may take effect before the end of the term of the rental agreement. Subsection (3)(b) cuts that to 30 days for a subsidized tenancy where the rent is based on the tenant's income or circumstances specific to the subsidized household.

RCW 59.18.720 also requires the notice to be on a form substantially the same as the one printed in that section, and service has to be in accordance with RCW 59.12.040. The right percentage on the wrong timeline is still defective.

Where an increase exceeds the cap on a claimed exemption, RCW 59.18.700(2) requires the supporting facts to appear in the notice itself. For a tenant holding a notice that claims an exemption and recites no facts, the statute put the obligation to state them on the landlord.

sections.heading: What happens if the increase is over the cap?

paras.p: RCW 59.18.700(3) puts one step on the tenant and separately gives the tenant a way out. The step is the demand to cure: where a landlord raises the rent above the limit without an exemption, the tenant must offer the landlord an opportunity to cure by providing a written demand to reduce the increase to a complying amount.

Separately, and in the statute's words in addition to any other remedy available under the chapter or other law, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement any time before the effective date of the increase on at least 20 days' written notice. A tenant who leaves that way owes rent for the full month in which the tenant vacates, and the landlord may not charge any fines or fees for terminating. Nothing in the subsection conditions that exit, the full-month rent rule, or the bar on fines and fees on the demand having gone out first.

paras.sub: Why withholding the increase is still the weaker move

paras.p: What the subsection does not give a tenant is the right to stay and pay less. It writes the cure demand as an obligation on the tenant, and RCW 59.18.700(5)(b) lets the attorney general sue without one while saying nothing of the kind about a tenant's own suit, so whether a tenant who skipped the demand keeps the damages remedy is not answered in the text. Continuing in possession after a default in the payment of rent is also cause to end a tenancy under RCW 59.18.650(2)(a), reached through the pay-or-vacate notice at RCW 59.18.057.

A renter can therefore be right about the increase and still end up litigating possession on the landlord's timetable. An owner who receives a demand is usually looking at the cheapest moment the dispute will offer, since curing down to the lawful number costs only the difference.

Declining to cure costs more. Under RCW 59.18.700(5)(a), where a court finds a violation of RCW 59.18.700, 59.18.710, 59.18.720 or 59.18.140, it shall award the tenant any excess rent, fees or other costs paid, up to three months of any unlawful rent, fees or other costs charged, and reasonable attorneys' fees and costs. The attorney general may sue without any cure offer at all, and may recover civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation.

sections.heading: Does the rent cap apply to my building?

paras.p: The exemptions in RCW 59.18.710 are categorical, not discretionary. The broadest is age of construction, because the cap does not limit increases for a unit whose first certificate of occupancy was issued 12 or fewer years before the date of the increase notice. Others turn on ownership, covering public housing and public development authority units, and nonprofit-owned or tax-credit units where maximum rents are already regulated.

The small-landlord exemptions get contested most. RCW 59.18.710(1)(e) through (g) cover a unit where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with a resident owner, an owner-occupied single-family residence where the owner rents no more than two units or bedrooms, and a duplex, triplex or fourplex where the owner occupied a unit as a principal residence when the tenancy began and still does.

Subsection (2) then withdraws all three where the owner is a real estate investment trust, a corporation, or a limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation. The member test is the whole of it. A duplex held in an LLC owned only by individuals keeps the exemption, and the same duplex held in an LLC with a corporate member does not.

sections.heading: Can a landlord evict without cause in Washington?

paras.p: Generally, no. RCW 59.18.650(1)(a) provides that a landlord may not evict a tenant, refuse to continue a tenancy, or end a periodic tenancy except for the causes enumerated in subsection (2), so ending a tenancy starts with identifying the cause, and each cause carries its own notice period. Nonpayment requires written notice to pay or surrender the premises for the period set in RCW 59.12.030(3). A substantial breach of a material lease term requires notice specifying the acts or omissions with a cure date at least 10 days out, and waste or nuisance supports a three-day notice to quit.

Two causes concern the owner's own plans, both on 90 days. A landlord may in good faith seek possession so the owner or immediate family can occupy the unit as a principal residence, but only where no substantially equivalent unit is vacant in the same building, and a bad-faith presumption arises if that person fails to occupy it for at least 60 consecutive days in the 90 days after the tenant left. An owner electing to sell a single-family residence may also end the tenancy on 90 days' notice, though the statute defines electing to sell by reference to listing within 30 days of the vacancy.

The two narrow routes to end a tenancy without cause are settled by how the lease was written at the outset. Under RCW 59.18.650(1)(b) a landlord may end a rollover tenancy at the end of the initial period only where the original agreement ran between six and 12 months, with at least 60 days' advance written notice. RCW 59.18.650(1)(c) covers a fixed term that does not roll over, and there the agreement has to have run 12 months or more, or successive agreements of six months or more continuously from the start, with the same 60 days' notice and no periodic interval at any point since the tenancy began. A nine-month fixed term satisfies neither route, so the ability is bought at signing.

sections.heading: Can my landlord lock me out?

paras.p: No, and this is one of the few places where the chapter is blunt. RCW 59.18.290(1) makes it unlawful for a landlord to remove or exclude a tenant except under a court order, and a tenant removed in violation of it may recover possession or terminate the rental agreement, and in either case recover actual damages, with costs and reasonable attorneys' fees to the prevailing party. Changing the locks commonly turns a case the owner was positioned to win into one the owner is defending, with the tenant choosing the remedy.

The section is not one-directional. Holding over or excluding the landlord after the agreement terminates without a court order is unlawful too, though subsection (3) bars a fee award to the landlord where the judgment followed the tenant's failure to respond, and again where the rent awarded is no more than two months of contract rent or $1,200, whichever is greater. Cutting off utilities is the other version of this move, and RCW 59.18.060(11)(a) bars terminating electric or water service for nonpayment on a day the national weather service has issued, or announced it will issue, a heat-related alert.

sections.heading: My landlord won't return my deposit

paras.p: RCW 59.18.280(1) gives the landlord 30 days from termination of the agreement and the tenant's vacating, and what is sent matters as much as when. The landlord must give a full and specific statement of the basis for retaining any of the deposit, with estimates or invoices substantiating the damage charges, plus any refund owed. Nothing may be withheld for wear from ordinary use, for carpet cleaning absent documented wear beyond ordinary use, or for fixtures, appliances and furnishings whose condition was never recorded in the checklist RCW 59.18.260 requires.

Missing that window is expensive. Under RCW 59.18.280(2) the landlord becomes liable for the full amount of the deposit and is barred from asserting any claim or defense for retaining it, absent circumstances beyond the landlord's control or an abandonment. Those are the provisions that give a deposit dispute its shape: the deposit itself is on the table, the court may add up to twice its amount where it finds the refusal was intentional, and the cost of suit and a reasonable attorneys' fee go to the prevailing party, which can be either side.

The section is not all one way. RCW 59.18.280(3)(a) preserves the landlord's right to proceed against a tenant for sums exceeding the deposit where the tenant is responsible for the damage, together with reasonable attorneys' fees, and RCW 59.18.280(4) exempts a deposit withheld for reasons unrelated to damage, such as rent owing, from the checklist and documentation requirements.

sections.heading: What is a deposit waiver fee, and what does agreeing to one change?

paras.p: RCW 59.18.670 lets a landlord waive the security deposit and take a monthly fee instead, used to buy insurance against the landlord's losses. It may be entirely or partially nonrefundable, so long as the lease discloses that and the tenant separately acknowledges it, and it must be strictly optional and offered to every approved applicant.

The capitalized part of the statutory disclosure is the part to read twice, because the tenant is neither an insured party nor a beneficiary under the policy and stays obligated for rent and for damage beyond ordinary wear. Cutting the other way, the fee is not rent, so failing to pay it is not cause for eviction under RCW 59.18.650, although the landlord may still sue to collect it.

sections.heading: Can my landlord raise the rent because I complained?

paras.p: RCW 59.18.240 provides that so long as the tenant is in compliance with the chapter, a landlord may not take or threaten reprisals for the tenant's good faith and lawful complaints to a governmental authority about a maintenance code failure that may endanger health or safety, or for a good faith and lawful assertion of rights under the chapter. Eviction, raising the rent, reducing services and increasing the tenant's obligations all count where intended primarily to retaliate, and RCW 59.18.250 adds that doing any of them within 90 days after the tenant's protected act creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation.

The same section gives the landlord three ways back. No presumption arises on a rent increase where the notice specifies reasonable grounds for it, which may include a substantial increase in market value due to remedial action under the chapter, so an owner raising rent near a complaint has a reason to state those grounds. The presumption runs the other way where the tenant was in arrears or in breach when the termination notice went out. And where the court finds the tenant complained within 90 days after notice of a proposed increase or other good faith action by the landlord, a rebuttable presumption runs that the complaint itself was not in good faith.
For a tenant, the mirror image is documenting both dates, since the 90 days moves the burden rather than deciding the case.

sections.heading: Who has to fix what?

paras.p: RCW 59.18.060 requires the landlord to keep the premises fit for human habitation throughout the tenancy, and its particulars run to code compliance where a condition endangers health or safety, structural components in reasonably good repair, and facilities adequate to supply heat and water and hot water. Pest control is two duties, a reasonable program at the start of the tenancy and, outside a single-family residence, control during it except where the tenant caused it.

RCW 59.18.130 sets the tenant's side, from paying rent as agreed to keeping the occupied portion clean and restoring the premises on vacating except for wear from ordinary use. A complaint about an item on the landlord's list is a complaint about a statutory duty, which is what can start the 90-day clock above.

sections.heading: How does an eviction actually work in court?

paras.p: An unlawful detainer action is a lawsuit, and what produces a lockout at the end of it is a writ of restitution. Under RCW 59.18.370 the plaintiff applies to the superior court for an order directing the defendant to appear and show cause why a writ should not issue, and the hearing the judge sets must be not less than seven nor more than 30 days from the date that order is served. For a tenant that hearing is often where the case is decided, and for an owner the same short timetable is why a defective notice is costly.

RCW 59.18.283 reverses what many leases assume: the landlord must apply any payment a tenant makes toward rent before late payments, damages or legal costs, and may not condition the right to possession on paying any amount other than rent, except as RCW 59.18.410 allows.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: Most of what decides these matters is documentary and happens before anyone files. Two different notices carry two different content rules. A rent increase notice takes the form in RCW 59.18.720, with the exemption facts stated where an exemption is claimed. A notice ending a tenancy has to name a cause from RCW 59.18.650 and, under RCW 59.18.650(6)(b), identify the facts and circumstances supporting it with enough specificity for the tenant to prepare a defense. Both are served under RCW 59.12.040, and the renter's work is reading whichever notice arrived against the rule it had to meet.

Fee-shifting is the other reason to get a read early. RCW 59.18.250, RCW 59.18.280 and RCW 59.18.290 shift costs and reasonable attorneys' fees either way, while RCW 59.18.700 shifts them one way only, to the tenant or the attorney general. I handle these matters from Spokane, for owners and for renters, though never for both sides of the same dispute. If you are holding a notice you do not understand, or about to send one, the time to have it looked at is before the clock inside it runs out. I represent clients throughout Washington.

paras.p: This article is general information about Washington law and is current as of the date it was published. It is not legal advice, and reading it does not create an attorney-client relationship. The Residential Landlord-Tenant Act changes, the maximum rent increase percentage published under RCW 59.18.700 is recalculated every year, and how any of this applies to a particular tenancy depends on facts an article cannot know. Speak with a lawyer about your own situation before acting on anything here.

title: USERRA in Washington: Reemployment Rights After Military Service
titleTag: USERRA Reemployment Rights in Washington | Justin D. Leigh
description: What USERRA requires when you leave a civilian job for military service, which position your employer has to put you back into, and why 38 U.S.C. 4327(b) sets no deadline to file. Plus what Washington law adds on top of it.
lede: Fairchild Air Force Base and the Washington Army and Air National Guard mean that many people around Spokane carry a civilian job and a military obligation at the same time. The federal law protecting that job is the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act, 38 U.S.C. sections 4301 through 4327. It gives a person who leaves work for service the right to go back, and names the position that has to be. Washington adds a veterans' employment chapter, and the Law Against Discrimination makes military status a protected class.
intro: The most useful thing in the statute is the thing almost nobody knows, so it goes first. Congress wrote into 38 U.S.C. 4327(b) that there is no limit on the period for filing a USERRA complaint or claim. People talk themselves out of these cases assuming it is too late.

sections.heading: How long do I have to file a USERRA claim?

paras.p: Section 4327(b) provides that if any person seeks to file a complaint or claim with the Secretary of Labor, the Merit Systems Protection Board, or a federal or state court alleging a violation of the chapter, "there shall be no limit on the period for filing the complaint or claim." Section 4327(a) adds that a federal official's missed deadline under section 4322, 4323, or 4324 gives the employer no defense, a limitations period included.

Nor does anything require going through the Department of Labor first, since section 4323(a)(3) permits an action where the person chose not to apply to the Secretary or was refused representation. On its own words 4327(b) governs claims under the federal chapter and says nothing about the timing of the Washington claims below. What the statute cannot do is preserve evidence. The filing period has no end, and the practical ability to prove what happened does.

sections.heading: Can I get my job back after a deployment?

paras.p: Section 4312(a) sets out the right. A person whose absence from a job is necessitated by service in the uniformed services is entitled to reemployment if advance written or verbal notice was given, the cumulative length of that absence and all earlier service absences with that employer does not exceed five years, and they report back in time. Section 4312(b) excuses notice where military necessity precludes it, or where giving it was otherwise impossible or unreasonable in the circumstances.

The five-year clock is narrower than it sounds. Section 4312(c) excludes service required beyond five years to finish an initial obligation, service a person could not get release orders from through no fault of their own, certain required training, and a long list of involuntary activations, declared war and national emergency among them. Someone mobilized repeatedly can have far less counted time than total time away.

One condition sits behind it. Section 4312(a) is expressly subject to section 4304, which ends entitlement on a dishonorable or bad conduct discharge, a separation under other than honorable conditions, or a dismissal or dropping from the rolls under 10 U.S.C. 1161. Character of service is the gate.

The employer's defenses are narrow. Section 4312(d)(1) excuses reemployment where its circumstances have so changed as to make it impossible or unreasonable, or where the job was for a brief, nonrecurrent period with no reasonable expectation of continuing indefinitely or for a significant period. Section 4312(d)(2) puts the burden of proving either on the employer.

sections.heading: Does a drill weekend count, or only a deployment?

paras.p: Section 4303(13) defines service in the uniformed services broadly, including active duty, active duty for training, inactive duty training, full-time National Guard duty, state active duty of fourteen days or more, a fitness examination, and funeral honors duty.

Section 4312(h) closes the question from the other side. The timing, frequency and duration of the service, or its nature including voluntary service, is not a basis for denying protection so long as the service stays inside the five-year limit, notice was given under subsection (a)(1), and the person reported back under subsection (e). RCW 73.16.031(12) includes state-ordered active duty, which the federal definition reaches only at fourteen days or more.

sections.heading: How fast do I have to report back to work?

paras.p: Section 4312(e)(1) sets four deadlines, and the right one depends on the service. A person whose service was under thirty-one days reports by the beginning of the first full regularly scheduled work period on the first full calendar day after it ends, once eight hours have passed for safe travel home, and a fitness examination takes the same timing. Service of more than thirty days but under one hundred eighty-one carries fourteen days to apply, and service of more than one hundred eighty days carries ninety. RCW 73.16.035(1)(c) sets the same ladder under the state chapter.

Illness and injury have their own rule. Section 4312(e)(2) lets a person hospitalized for or convalescing from an illness or injury incurred in or aggravated during service report at the end of the recovery period, caps that at two years, and extends it for circumstances beyond their control.

Missing a deadline is not fatal. Section 4312(e)(3) provides that a person who reports late does not automatically forfeit the chapter's rights, but becomes subject to the employer's ordinary discipline for absence. Section 4312(f)(4) bars an employer from defeating a reemployment obligation by demanding documentation that does not then exist. RCW 73.16.035 carries both rules.

sections.heading: Do they have to give me my old job, or can they put me anywhere?

paras.p: Section 4313 is misread most often, because it does not promise the old job. For service of more than ninety days, section 4313(a)(2) puts the person in the position they would have held had the employment not been interrupted, or one of like seniority, status and pay, if they are qualified.

Shorter service is governed by section 4313(a)(1), and it is narrower rather than the same. The employer owes the position the person would have held, and may fall back to the job held when the service began only if the person is not qualified for the first after reasonable efforts to qualify them. A sixty-day activation does not let the employer hand back a comparable job.

That phrase, the position in which the person would have been employed, is the escalator. The statute treats the service member as though they had been on a moving staircase the whole time they were gone. If a step increase would have come due, or the classification was reorganized into a higher grade, the position the statute names is the one at the top rather than the one they stepped off, if they are qualified to perform its duties.

Two definitions matter. Section 4303(9) defines qualified as the ability to perform the essential tasks of the position, and section 4303(10) defines reasonable efforts as employer actions, training included, that do not impose an undue hardship on the employer. So a lack of training for the upgraded job is not on its own an answer. The employer owes those efforts, and under section 4313(a)(2)(B) may fall back to the earlier position only where the person is still not qualified afterward.

Where a service-related disability blocks that position even after accommodation, section 4313(a)(3) calls for the nearest equivalent to it. RCW 73.16.033 states Washington's version more plainly, requiring reemployment forthwith to the former position or one of like seniority, status and pay.

sections.heading: Do I lose my health insurance while I am gone?

paras.p: Not if the person elects to keep it. Section 4317(a) requires a health plan covering a person through the job to let that person elect to continue it during an absence for service, for the lesser of twenty-four months from the start of the absence or the day after the person fails to return under section 4312(e). The plan may charge up to 102 percent of the full premium, except that someone serving under thirty-one days pays no more than the employee share.

Coming back is protected separately. Section 4317(b)(1) bars any exclusion or waiting period on reinstated coverage that would not have applied had it never lapsed, and it covers the family members whose coverage returns with the employee's. Section 4317(b)(2) carves out one thing, coverage of an illness or injury the Secretary of Veterans Affairs determines was incurred in, or aggravated during, the service.

sections.heading: What happens to my seniority, benefits and pension while I am gone?

paras.p: Section 4316(b)(1) deems a person absent for service to be on furlough or leave of absence, and entitles them to the rights and benefits not determined by seniority that the employer generally provides to employees of similar seniority, status and pay who are on leave. The benchmark is what the employer does for others on leave. One exception sits in section 4316(b)(2), where a person who knowingly gives clear written notice of intent not to return loses those benefits and the employer must prove the notice was given that way. Paid leave is the employee's call: section 4316(d) lets a person use accrued vacation during the service and bars an employer from requiring it.

Section 4318 handles pensions by treating the gap as though it were not there. A reemployed person is treated as not having incurred a break in service, and each period of service counts with the plan's employer for vesting and accrual. The employer funds that, while benefits turning on employee contributions are owed only as the person pays them in.

sections.heading: Can I be fired after coming back from deployment?

paras.p: Only for cause, for a period after the return that depends on the service. Section 4316(c) provides that a reemployed person shall not be discharged except for cause within one year of reemployment where the prior service exceeded one hundred eighty days, or within one hundred eighty days where it ran more than thirty but under one hundred eighty-one. RCW 73.16.051 bars discharge without cause within one year of restoration. Inside that window the employer needs a reason.

sections.heading: They did not fire me, they just stopped promoting me

paras.p: Section 4311(a) prohibits an employer from denying initial employment, reemployment, retention, promotion or any benefit of employment because of a person's membership in, performance of, or obligation to perform service. Because the status includes merely having an obligation, someone never activated is covered.

Section 4311(c)(1) sets the causation standard. The employer has violated the section if the person's service or obligation was a motivating factor, unless the employer can prove it would have acted the same way anyway. RCW 73.16.032(1) and (3)(a) adopt the same prohibition and framework.

paras.sub: Retaliation reaches people who never served

paras.p: Section 4311(b) bars an employer from taking any adverse employment action or other retaliatory action against a person because they enforced a protection under the chapter, testified in a proceeding, assisted in an investigation, or exercised a right. Its last sentence matters, because the prohibition applies whether or not the person has served. The coworker who writes a statement supporting a reservist's complaint is protected though he never wore a uniform, and RCW 73.16.032(2) carries the same rule.

sections.heading: My employer will not take me back after the Guard. What are my options?

paras.p: There are three federal routes, and the first is the gateway to the second. Section 4322 lets a person file a written complaint with the Secretary of Labor naming the employer and summarizing the allegations, and the Secretary must notify the person of their rights within five days, investigate, and finish within ninety days. Where the Secretary cannot resolve it, section 4323(a)(1) lets the person ask that it go to the Attorney General, who has sixty days under section 4323(a)(2) to decide whether to appear. That route runs through the Secretary, not around. Section 4321 separately directs the Secretary, through the Veterans' Employment and Training Service, to assist any person with the chapter's rights.

The third route is to sue directly under section 4323(a)(3). Section 4323(b) gives the federal district courts jurisdiction over an action against a private employer, while one against a state as employer may be brought in state court. Section 4323(i) defines private employer there to include a political subdivision of a state, which matters to city and county employees. Federal employees go to the Merit Systems Protection Board under section 4324.

sections.heading: What can a court actually order?

paras.p: Section 4323(d) lets a court order the employer to comply, compensate the person for any loss of wages or benefits, and pay interest at three percent per year. Where the court finds the employer knowingly failed to comply, section 4323(d)(1)(D) allows liquidated damages of fifty thousand dollars or the compensation and interest already awarded, whichever is greater. Fees then run in the claimant's favor, because section 4323(h)(1) bars taxing fees or costs against a claimant and section 4323(h)(2) requires an award of reasonable fees and expenses to a person who prevails in a private action.

sections.heading: Does Washington law give me anything federal law does not?

paras.p: The most practical thing in chapter 73.16 RCW is one sentence. RCW 73.16.070 declares that the federal act applies in proper cases in all the courts of this state, so a USERRA claim is not confined to federal court. RCW 73.16.035(5) puts the burden of proving impossibility, undue hardship, or a temporary position on the employer, and RCW 73.16.090 preserves any more beneficial right under another law or a contract.

The chapter sets conditions of its own. A person must have notified the employer of membership in the uniformed services within a reasonable time of taking the job or joining, and RCW 73.16.035(1)(a) bars retaliation for that notice. State-ordered active duty carries a limit of twelve weeks in a calendar year under RCW 73.16.035(1)(f), extendable to twelve months in a declared emergency.

sections.heading: Who enforces the Washington chapter?

paras.p: The state route is narrower and the limits sit on the face of the statute. RCW 73.16.061(1) requires the Washington attorney general to sue in superior court for compliance and lost wages, but only where the service was state duty not covered by USERRA and the adjutant general has asked the employer about it without result. RCW 73.16.061(2) then lets a person use private counsel instead.

RCW 73.16.100 bears reading too. It declares that the public policies articulated in chapter 133, Laws of 2001 depend on procedures established in that act, and that no civil or criminal action may be maintained on those policies without complying with the chapter's procedures.

sections.heading: Is military status a protected class in Washington?

paras.p: It is, under a different statute with its own remedies. RCW 49.60.030(1) declares freedom from discrimination because of honorably discharged veteran or military status a civil right, listing first the right to obtain and hold employment. RCW 49.60.180 makes it an unfair practice for an employer to refuse to hire, to discharge or bar from employment, or to discriminate in the terms of employment on that basis.

The phrase is broader than its label. RCW 49.60.040(15) defines honorably discharged veteran or military status as a person who is either a veteran as defined in RCW 41.04.007, or an active or reserve member of any branch of the armed forces, including the national guard, coast guard and reserves. A reservist never discharged from anything is in the protected class under that second prong.

RCW 49.60.030(2) then gives a person injured by a violation of the chapter a civil action to enjoin further violations, to recover actual damages, or both, with the cost of suit and reasonable attorneys' fees.

One limit matters early, and it runs the opposite way from what people assume. The Law Against Discrimination reaches only an employer of eight or more persons under RCW 49.60.040(11), so the RCW 49.60.180 route is closed against a smaller one. Chapter 73.16 RCW carries no employee-count floor at all, and for a short state activation, which RCW 73.16.031(12) covers and 4303(13) reaches only at fourteen days or more, the state chapter is the claim and the federal one is not. What narrows that route is RCW 73.16.061, not size.

sections.heading: My union contract gives me more than the statute. Which one controls?

paras.p: The more generous term controls. Section 4302(a) provides that nothing in the chapter diminishes a law, contract or policy establishing a right more beneficial than the chapter's, so a union contract with a longer reinstatement window survives USERRA untouched. Section 4302(b) runs the other way, superseding anything that reduces or eliminates a right the chapter provides.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: Most of the work in a reemployment case is reconstruction rather than argument. The orders and the unit's records establish what kind of duty was performed. They also establish how much of it counts against the five-year limit once the 4312(c) exclusions are applied. Working out where the escalator would have carried somebody under section 4313 means pulling the job's promotion history and who else moved and when, which is also what makes the section 4323(d) wage calculation possible.

On the employer side the first question is usually whether section 4312(d) applies at all. After that it is what cause means inside the section 4316(c) window, and how far a documentation request can go under section 4312(f).

I handle USERRA and military-status employment matters from my office in downtown Spokane, for service members and for employers working out what the statute requires before the person reports back. I am admitted in Washington and Oregon, WSBA #55307 and OSB #242384. I represent clients throughout Washington.

paras.p: This article is general information about federal and Washington law, current as of publication. Provisions on both sides were amended recently, the federal ones by Public Law 118-210 in January 2025 and chapter 73.16 RCW by the Laws of 2026, and the law keeps moving. title: Motorcycle Accidents in Washington: The Lane, the Helmet Argument, and the Coverage Nobody Told You to Buy
titleTag: Motorcycle Accident Lawyer in Spokane, WA | Justin D. Leigh
description: Washington gives a motorcycle the whole lane, bans lane splitting, and leaves riders out of the underinsured motorist coverage every car policy has to carry. What that means for your claim.
lede: A driver turned left across your lane on Division and told the officer the same thing every one of them says, which is that they never saw you. You are out of the hospital with hardware in your leg, the bike is a total loss, and somebody from the driver's insurance company has already asked whether you were wearing a helmet and how fast you were going. There are two fights in a motorcycle case. One is about what happened in the intersection, and the other is about whether anybody will pay for it, and the second one turns on a line in the insurance code that most riders have never been shown.

sections.heading: A motorcycle is entitled to the whole lane, and that is a statute

paras.p: Drivers treat a motorcycle as half a vehicle. The law does not. RCW 46.61.608(1) says all motorcycles are entitled to full use of a lane and that no motor vehicle shall be driven in such a manner as to deprive any motorcycle of the full use of a lane. The one exception written into the subsection is two motorcycles riding abreast in a single lane, which the statute permits and then caps at two by RCW 46.61.608(4).

That matters at the moment a driver drifts over to share your lane, squeezes past you at a merge, or crowds you to the fog line because you were only taking up a few feet of it. None of that is a courtesy question. It is a right of way the Legislature gave you in writing.

The passing rules carry the same judgment. RCW 46.61.110(1)(b) says that when the vehicle being overtaken is a motorcycle, a driver who fails to pass at a safe distance is assessed an additional fine on top of the base penalty, and that the fine may not be waived, reduced, or suspended unless the court finds the driver indigent. A traffic fine is not civil liability and no infraction decides your claim. What it tells you is how seriously the statute treats the risk a passing car creates for the person on the bike.

sections.heading: Is lane splitting legal in Washington?

paras.p: No. RCW 46.61.608(3) says no person shall operate a motorcycle between lanes of traffic or between adjacent lines or rows of vehicles. RCW 46.61.608(2) separately forbids overtaking and passing in the same lane as the vehicle being overtaken, with a narrow carve-out for passing a pedestrian or a bicyclist at a safe distance of at least three feet. Subsection (5) exempts police officers on duty, and nobody else.

Riders ask this because they have been told that splitting between stopped cars is safer than sitting in the middle of them, and because it is lawful in other states. In Washington it is not, and a crash that happens while you are between two lines of cars is a harder case.

Harder is not hopeless, and the reason is worth understanding. RCW 5.40.050 provides that breaking a statute, ordinance, or administrative rule is not negligence per se but may be considered by the trier of fact as evidence of negligence. The section lists four exceptions that still are negligence per se, and the traffic one is driving under the influence. Lane splitting is not on that list. So the violation is evidence a jury weighs against everything else in the case, not an automatic verdict.

sections.heading: Do I lose my case if I was not wearing a helmet?

paras.p: Washington requires one. RCW 46.37.530(1)(c) makes it unlawful to operate or ride on a motorcycle on a state highway, county road, or city street without a motorcycle helmet, with the neck or chin strap fastened securely while the motorcycle is in motion. RCW 46.37.530(3) defines the helmet by federal standard: a hard outer shell, padding, a retention system, and the manufacturer's certification under 49 C.F.R. 571.218 that it meets the United States Department of Transportation standard. A novelty shell is not a helmet under that definition.

Now the part the adjuster is counting on you not knowing. Washington's seat belt statute, RCW 46.61.688(6), says in so many words that failing to wear a safety belt does not constitute negligence and may not be admissible as evidence of negligence in any civil action. The helmet statute contains no provision like it. That silence is why the argument gets made, and it is why the answer is not a clean one in either direction.

What can be said accurately is this. Not wearing a helmet does not bar a claim, because Washington is a comparative fault state and fault reduces an award rather than ending it. Under RCW 5.40.050 a breach of the helmet statute would be evidence of negligence rather than negligence per se. And whether that evidence has anything to do with the injuries actually in dispute is a separate question, because a helmet has no bearing on a shattered femur. Expect the argument. Do not accept it as the end of the conversation, and do not let a recorded statement on day one be where it gets decided.

sections.heading: Being partly at fault does not end your claim

paras.p: RCW 4.22.005 is the rule the whole system runs on: contributory fault chargeable to the claimant diminishes the award proportionately, but does not bar recovery. If a jury finds you twenty percent responsible, your award is reduced by twenty percent. It is not zero, and Washington has no threshold at which it becomes zero.

Fault is defined broadly by RCW 4.22.015, reaching negligent and reckless acts and omissions, unreasonable assumption of risk, and the unreasonable failure to avoid an injury or to mitigate damages. The same section says a comparison of fault considers both the nature of the conduct and the extent of its causal relation to the damages, which is the sentence that answers a defense built on speed or gear rather than on what caused the collision.

RCW 4.22.070 then has the jury assign a percentage to every entity that caused the damages, including you, and makes each defendant liable for its own share only. There is one exception that matters to riders: under RCW 4.22.070(1)(b), if the trier of fact finds the injured person was not at fault, the defendants are jointly and severally liable for the sum of their shares. That is why a case in which the rider bears no fault is in a different posture from the same injuries with a fault argument attached, and not only because of the percentage.

sections.heading: The coverage nobody told you to buy

paras.p: This is the part of a motorcycle case that surprises people, and it is a single clause. RCW 48.22.030(2) requires every auto policy issued in Washington to carry underinsured motorist coverage, which is the coverage that pays when the at-fault driver has no insurance or not enough of it. Then it writes an exception into the middle of the sentence: except while operating or occupying a motorcycle or motor-driven cycle.

So the protection a car owner gets automatically unless they reject it in writing does not follow a rider onto the bike. The Legislature's answer was disclosure rather than coverage. RCW 48.22.030(9) requires an insurer that writes motorcycle insurance in this state to provide information to prospective insureds about the coverage, and RCW 48.22.030(10) requires it to give a named insured who bought motorcycle liability coverage an opportunity to reject underinsured coverage for that motorcycle in writing.

Personal injury protection runs the same way. RCW 48.22.085(1) requires PIP to be offered as an optional coverage on an automobile liability policy, and RCW 48.22.005(1) defines automobile as a passenger car under RCW 46.04.382. A motorcycle is not a passenger car. So do not assume the medical coverage that a car policy carries is sitting behind your bike.

The practical consequence is blunt. Washington's minimum liability limits are frequently not enough for a serious orthopedic injury, and when the driver who turned in front of you carries the minimum, underinsured motorist coverage on your own motorcycle policy is frequently the only money in the case. Pull the declarations page before you decide anything. If the coverage is there, there is somewhere else to look for payment. If you rejected it, you want to know that in week one rather than in month nine.

sections.heading: The car that never touched you

paras.p: A great many motorcycle crashes involve no contact at all. A car crosses the line, you lay it down avoiding the car, the car keeps going, and there is no paint transfer and no plate number. Washington has a name for that vehicle and a route to coverage for it.

RCW 48.22.030(8) defines a phantom vehicle as a motor vehicle that causes bodily injury, death, or property damage to an insured without physical contact with the insured or the vehicle the insured was occupying, and then attaches two conditions. The facts of the accident must be corroborated by competent evidence other than the testimony of the insured or anyone else with an underinsured motorist claim from the same accident. And the accident must be reported to the appropriate law enforcement agency within seventy-two hours.

Seventy-two hours is a real deadline and it runs while you are in a hospital bed. If nobody files a report, the phantom vehicle claim is in trouble no matter how true the account is. The corroboration requirement is the other half of it, which is why the names of the people who stopped at the scene are worth more than almost anything else you can collect that day.

sections.heading: How long do I have to bring a motorcycle accident claim in Washington?

paras.p: Three years. RCW 4.16.080(2) sets a three-year limit for any other injury to the person or rights of another, and a motorcycle injury claim runs under it from the date of the crash.

RCW 4.16.190 takes the time a claimant was under eighteen out of the limitation period, so a passenger who was a minor is on a different clock than the rider. That is a reason to check rather than a reason to wait.

If the other vehicle belonged to a city, a county, a transit agency, or the state, there is a separate claim you have to present before you can file suit at all, and the deadline for it is much shorter than three years. That one is covered in the article on claims against government entities.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The recorded statement in the first week, taken while you are on pain medication, in which the questions are about speed, gear, and how long you have been riding rather than about the left turn.
Nobody reports the phantom vehicle inside seventy-two hours, and the only evidence that it existed is the rider's own account, which RCW 48.22.030(8)(a) says is not enough on its own.

The bike gets released to salvage before anyone photographs it or downloads anything from it. The motorcycle is evidence of the impact and of how the crash happened, and a tow yard will dispose of it on its own schedule.
No one ever looks at the rider's own declarations page, so a case settles against a minimum limits liability policy while underinsured motorist coverage sits unused on the motorcycle policy.
Gear gets thrown away. The helmet, the jacket, the boots and the abrasions on all three are the physical record of what the body absorbed, and they photograph in a way that a chart note does not.
Settling before the orthopedic picture is finished. Hardware gets removed, nonunions declare themselves, and the long-term cost of a crushed ankle is not knowable at eight weeks.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: Most of the useful work happens early. Getting the collision report and the names of the witnesses while they are still reachable. Putting a hold on the motorcycle before the yard crushes it. Reading every policy in reach, yours included, because the carve-out in RCW 48.22.030(2) means the answer to who pays is often found on your own declarations page rather than the other driver's. Keeping you off the phone with an adjuster whose first three questions are about your helmet. And making the liability case out of the physical evidence instead of out of a contest between two drivers' memories, because the version of events that gets written down in the first month tends to be the version everybody argues about for the next two years.

title: Hit While Walking in Washington: The Crosswalk You Did Not Know You Were Standing In
titleTag: Pedestrian Accident Lawyer in Spokane, WA | Justin D. Leigh
description: Washington law puts a crosswalk at nearly every intersection whether or not anybody painted one, and tells drivers to stop and stay stopped. What that means if a car hit you, and where the money comes from.
lede: You were crossing at the corner where you always cross, the one with no painted lines, and a car turning right never slowed down. Now you are at Sacred Heart with a tibial plateau fracture, the officer's report says you were not in a crosswalk, and an adjuster has already used the word jaywalking. That report may be wrong about the law. Washington puts a crosswalk at nearly every intersection in the state whether or not anybody ever painted one.

sections.heading: An unmarked crosswalk is still a crosswalk

paras.p: RCW 46.04.160 defines crosswalk as the portion of the roadway between the intersection area and a prolongation or connection of the farthest sidewalk line, and then adds the part people never hear: if there are no sidewalks, the crosswalk is the portion between the intersection area and a line ten feet from it. A marked crosswalk modifies that, but it does not create it.

Read plainly, that means the invisible continuation of the sidewalk across the street is a legal crosswalk. So is a ten-foot band at an intersection with no sidewalks at all. The paint is a convenience for drivers, not the thing that gives a person on foot the right of way.

This single definition decides a surprising number of cases, because the word jaywalking appears in a collision report whenever a pedestrian was not standing between two painted lines. Where the person was actually standing, measured against RCW 46.04.160, is a question of fact that nobody usually asks on the night it happens.

sections.heading: What the driver was required to do

paras.p: RCW 46.61.235(1) says the operator of an approaching vehicle shall stop and remain stopped to allow a pedestrian to cross the roadway within an unmarked or marked crosswalk when the pedestrian is upon or within one lane of the half of the roadway the vehicle is traveling on, or onto which it is turning. The statute defines half of the roadway as all lanes carrying traffic in one direction, and the entire width of a one-way street.

Two phrases there do work. Stop and remain stopped is not yield. And within one lane of sets the trigger distance, which is why a driver who claims the pedestrian came out of nowhere is often describing a duty that had already attached a lane earlier.

RCW 46.61.235(4) adds the rule that catches the second car. When any vehicle is stopped at a crosswalk to let a pedestrian cross, a driver approaching from behind may not overtake and pass that stopped vehicle. The car that stops is also the car that hides you from the one behind it.

On the sidewalk the rule is simpler still. RCW 46.61.261(1) says the driver of a vehicle shall yield the right of way to any pedestrian on a sidewalk, which is the provision that governs the car coming out of a parking garage or across a driveway apron.

sections.heading: When the pedestrian is the one who has to yield

paras.p: Honest answer: there are real limits, and an adjuster who knows them will use them.

RCW 46.61.240(1) says a pedestrian crossing a roadway at any point other than within a marked crosswalk, or within an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection, shall yield the right of way to all vehicles on the roadway. Mid-block crossings are where that bites. RCW 46.61.240(4) goes further between adjacent intersections where traffic-control signals are in operation, and requires crossing only in a marked crosswalk. RCW 46.61.240(3) requires yielding where a pedestrian tunnel or overhead crossing exists, and (5) and (6) address diagonal crossing and crossings where a sign prohibits it.

RCW 46.61.235(2) is the other one. A pedestrian shall not suddenly leave a curb or other place of safety and move into the path of a vehicle that is so close it is impossible for the driver to stop. Note the actual standard, which is impossible rather than inconvenient or surprising.

There is also a provision written for people the rest of the chapter tends to forget. Under RCW 46.61.240(2), where curb ramps exist at or adjacent to intersections or at marked crosswalks elsewhere, persons with disabilities may enter the roadway from the curb ramps and cross within or as closely as practicable to the crosswalk.

sections.heading: Being partly in the wrong does not end your claim

paras.p: Even where one of those provisions applies, the consequence is not what people assume. RCW 4.22.005 says contributory fault diminishes the award proportionately but does not bar recovery. There is no percentage at which a Washington claim switches off.

And a breach of a traffic statute is not the end of the analysis either. RCW 5.40.050 provides that breaking a statute, ordinance, or administrative rule is not negligence per se but may be considered as evidence of negligence, with four listed exceptions, the traffic one being driving under the influence. So crossing outside a crosswalk is evidence a jury weighs. It is not a verdict.

RCW 4.22.015 tells the jury to weigh both the nature of the conduct and the extent of its causal relation to the damages. A driver doing forty-five in a thirty while looking at a phone and a person crossing twenty feet from the corner are not the same kind of fault, and the statute says so.

sections.heading: Where the money comes from when you were on foot

paras.p: A pedestrian has no vehicle damage claim and often assumes that means the only insurance in the case is the driver's. Frequently that is wrong, and the mistake is expensive.

Personal injury protection on an automobile policy is medical coverage that pays regardless of fault, and it commonly reaches the named insured and family members who are struck as pedestrians. RCW 48.22.085(1) requires PIP to be offered as an optional coverage on every automobile liability policy issued or renewed in this state, and RCW 48.22.085(2) says a named insured may reject it in writing. Whether it reaches you as a pedestrian is a question of the policy language, so the declarations page and the policy itself are worth pulling even if your own car was parked at home.

Underinsured motorist coverage is the other one, and it matters most when the driver who hit you carries Washington's minimum limits. RCW 48.22.030(2) requires that coverage on auto policies issued here, with an exception for a person operating or occupying a motorcycle and an exception for a vehicle owned by the household and not insured on the policy. A pedestrian is in neither exception.

If the driver left, RCW 48.22.030(2) reaches hit-and-run vehicles as well. And if no car ever touched you, RCW 48.22.030(8) defines a phantom vehicle and sets two conditions: the facts must be corroborated by competent evidence other than your own testimony, and the accident must be reported to the appropriate law enforcement agency within seventy-two hours.

sections.heading: How long do I have to sue after being hit by a car as a pedestrian?

paras.p: Three years. RCW 4.16.080(2) sets a three-year limit for any other injury to the person or rights of another, running from the date you were hit.
RCW 4.16.190 takes the time a claimant was under eighteen out of the limitation period, which matters because a large share of pedestrian injuries happen to children walking to school.

If the vehicle was a city bus, a county truck, a school district van, or a state vehicle, there is a claim you must present before you are allowed to file suit, and that deadline is far shorter. The article on claims against government entities covers it. RCW 46.61.235(5) is worth knowing too: an infraction committed in a school, playground, or crosswalk speed zone carries double the usual monetary penalty, and the penalty may not be waived, reduced, or suspended.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The collision report says the pedestrian was not in a crosswalk, nobody measures the location against RCW 46.04.160, and the word jaywalking survives into the claim file as if it were a finding.

No photographs of the intersection. Whether there is a sidewalk, where its lines would continue, how far the curb ramp sits from the corner, and what a turning driver could actually see are all answerable from the scene and almost unanswerable later.

The pedestrian gives a recorded statement describing where they thought they were, in a parking lot they have crossed a thousand times, without ever having looked at the statute that defines where they actually were.
Nobody pulls the household auto policies, so a claim is valued against a minimum limits liability policy while PIP and underinsured motorist coverage sit unexamined.
The no-contact case is never reported to police inside seventy-two hours, and RCW 48.22.030(8) then supplies the reason the carrier denies it.
Settling before the orthopedic outcome is known. Pedestrians struck by cars take lower-leg and pelvic injuries that look one way at six weeks and another way after a second surgery.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: The early work is mostly about the intersection and the policies. Getting out to the scene and documenting where the sidewalk lines run, where the curb ramps are, and what the sight line was for a turning driver. Pulling any camera that looks at the corner, because business and transit video is routinely overwritten inside a month. Finding every policy that might reach you, including the ones on cars you were not in. Reading the collision report against the statutes instead of accepting its conclusions, since an officer's narrative is evidence and not a ruling. And telling you honestly where RCW 46.61.240 is a genuine problem in your case, because that answer changes what the claim is worth and you should hear it from your own lawyer first.
