title: Bicycle Accidents in Washington: Where You Are Allowed to Ride, the Passing Rule, and Who Pays
titleTag: Bicycle Accident Lawyer in Spokane, WA | Justin D. Leigh
description: Washington gives a cyclist the rights and duties of a driver, lets you leave the right edge for four listed reasons, and in 2025 rewrote how a car must pass you. What that means after a crash.
lede: A driver came past you close enough to move the air, then turned right across your front wheel, and told the responding officer that you came out of nowhere and that bikes belong on the sidewalk. You are at the emergency department with a broken collarbone and a frame that is now scrap. Almost everything a driver believes about where a bicycle is allowed to be is written down in Washington, and most of it is the opposite of what they told the officer.

sections.heading: A bicycle on the roadway has the rights and the duties of a vehicle

paras.p: RCW 46.61.755(1) says every person riding a bicycle upon a roadway shall be granted all of the rights and shall be subject to all of the duties applicable to the driver of a vehicle, except for the special bicycle regulations in RCW 46.61.750 through 46.61.780 and except for provisions that by their nature cannot apply.

That is the whole frame of a bicycle case. You are not a guest in the lane. The driver owed you what they owed any other vehicle, and the right-of-way rules that would govern a car turning across your path govern that same turn across a bicycle.

RCW 46.61.755(2) handles the other half. A person riding on a sidewalk or crosswalk is granted all the rights and subject to all the duties of a pedestrian. So the cyclist on a sidewalk is not an outlaw, and RCW 46.61.261(1) requires drivers to yield to a bicycle on a sidewalk, while requiring the rider to yield to pedestrians there.

sections.heading: How far right do I actually have to ride?

paras.p: This is the argument in most of these cases, and RCW 46.61.770(1) answers it. A cyclist moving slower than the normal flow of traffic rides as near to the right side of the right through lane as is safe, with four exceptions written into the statute.

You may leave the right edge while preparing to turn or turning. You may use a dedicated right turn lane when approaching an intersection where right turns are permitted, even if you do not intend to turn right. You may move left while overtaking another bicycle or vehicle. And under subsection (1)(d), you may move when reasonably necessary to avoid unsafe conditions, which the statute defines to include fixed or moving objects, parked or moving vehicles, bicyclists, pedestrians, animals, and surface hazards.

That fourth exception is broad and it is what a door zone, a storm grate, broken pavement, or a row of parked cars falls under. RCW 46.61.770(3) separately permits use of the shoulder or any designated bicycle lane, and RCW 46.61.770(4) tells a rider in a single narrow lane to move far enough right to facilitate an overtaking vehicle unless conditions make that unsafe. RCW 46.61.770(5) allows riding two abreast, and no more than two, except on paths set aside for bicycles.

sections.heading: The three-foot rule, and what the Legislature changed in 2025

paras.p: RCW 46.61.110(2) governs a driver overtaking a person on a bicycle in the right lane, on the right shoulder, or in a bicycle lane, and it was amended most recently in 2025.

On a roadway with two or more lanes going the driver's direction, the driver must move completely into a lane to the left of the right lane before passing, and stay there until safely clear. That is not a suggestion to give room. It is a lane change.

On a road with only one lane in the direction of travel, the driver must reduce to a speed that is safe for passing relative to the cyclist's speed and pass at a safe distance, where practicable of at least three feet, to clearly avoid contact. If there is not enough room on the left to do that, the driver must move completely into the oncoming lane when it is safe and lawful to do so.

RCW 46.61.110(2)(b) adds a fine equal to the base penalty on top of it, unwaivable except on a finding of indigency, and (c) sends it to the vulnerable roadway user education account. A traffic fine is not civil liability and no infraction decides a claim, but the standard of care in that subsection is written in unusually concrete terms, and concrete is what a liability case runs on.

sections.heading: What about the helmet, the lights, and the sidewalk?

paras.p: Expect all three to be raised and none of them to be what the insurer suggests.

Washington's helmet statute, RCW 46.37.530, is written for motorcycles, mopeds, and motor-driven cycles. Where it mentions bicycles it does so by pointing outward, directing riders of electric-assisted bicycles and motorized foot scooters to comply with laws and regulations related to the use of bicycle helmets. Whether a helmet was required where you were riding is therefore a local ordinance question that differs by city and county, and it is worth checking against the actual ordinance rather than against what anybody assumes.

Equipment and sidewalk rules work the same way as every other traffic statute here. Under RCW 5.40.050, breaking a statute, ordinance, or administrative rule is not negligence per se but may be considered as evidence of negligence, and the four exceptions that remain negligence per se do not include anything about bicycles. So riding without a light after dark is evidence a jury weighs against the rest of the case.

And under RCW 4.22.005, contributory fault reduces an award proportionately and does not bar it. A rider found twenty percent at fault recovers eighty percent. RCW 4.22.015 directs the comparison to consider both the nature of the conduct and how much it actually caused, which is the answer to a defense built on a missing taillight in a daylight collision.

sections.heading: Who pays when a car hits a bicycle

paras.p: The driver's liability policy is the obvious one and it is frequently not enough. Washington's minimum limits are often well short of what a surgically repaired clavicle, a head injury, or three months away from work actually costs.

So look at your own auto policy even though you were on a bicycle. RCW 48.22.030(2) requires underinsured motorist coverage on auto policies issued in this state, reaching underinsured vehicles, hit-and-run vehicles, and phantom vehicles. The statute writes in an exception for a person operating or occupying a motorcycle or motor-driven cycle. A bicycle is neither, so that carve-out does not reach a cyclist.

Personal injury protection is the medical side of the same page. RCW 48.22.085(1) requires it to be offered as an optional coverage on every automobile liability policy issued or renewed here, and RCW 48.22.085(2) lets a named insured reject it in writing. Whether it reaches you while you are on a bicycle depends on the policy language, which is a reason to read the policy rather than guess at it.

If the car never touched you, which is common when a driver forces a rider into a curb or a ditch, RCW 48.22.030(8) is the provision to know. A phantom vehicle claim requires that the facts be corroborated by competent evidence other than your own testimony, and that the accident be reported to the appropriate law enforcement agency within seventy-two hours. Both conditions are easy to fail while you are still in a hospital.

sections.heading: How long do I have to bring a bicycle accident claim in Washington?

paras.p: Three years, under RCW 4.16.080(2), which sets a three-year limit for any other injury to the person or rights of another and runs from the date of the crash.
RCW 4.16.190 excludes from the limitation period the time a claimant was under eighteen. A great many bicycle injuries are to children, and their clock is not their parents' clock.

A claim against a city, county, transit agency, or the state has a separate step before suit and a much shorter deadline for it, which the article on claims against government entities covers. That is the ordinary posture for a crash caused by road surface or by a trail or bike lane design.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The bicycle is thrown away. The frame, the wheel, and the damaged components record the direction and force of the impact, and they are evidence long after the bruises are gone.
Nobody preserves the data. A bike computer, a phone, or a watch often holds speed and position in the seconds before the crash, and that record is usually the only neutral witness.
The collision report repeats the driver's belief that bikes are not allowed in the lane, nobody checks it against RCW 46.61.755 and RCW 46.61.770, and that belief becomes the frame of the claim.
The no-contact case goes unreported for more than seventy-two hours, which is exactly what RCW 48.22.030(8)(b) requires.
A head injury is treated as resolved because the CT was clean. Post-concussive symptoms declare themselves over months and belong in the medical record as they do.
No one reads the rider's own auto policy, and the case settles against the driver's minimum limits while underinsured motorist coverage sits unused.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: Early work decides most of these. Getting the bicycle and the gear into storage before anybody discards them. Pulling device data while it exists. Finding the business or transit camera that sees the intersection, which is normally overwritten inside a month. Reading the collision report against RCW 46.61.755 and RCW 46.61.770 rather than accepting its conclusions, because an officer's narrative is evidence and not a ruling on the law. Locating every policy that reaches you, including those on cars you were not riding in. And giving you a straight answer about where your own conduct is a real problem in the case rather than a bluff, since that is what the claim is actually worth.

title: Slip and Fall in Washington: Notice, Obvious Dangers, and the Ice in the Parking Lot
titleTag: Slip and Fall Lawyer in Spokane, WA | Justin D. Leigh
description: A Washington slip and fall usually turns on notice: whether the owner knew or should have known. The exceptions, the rule about obvious hazards, and why Washington refused to adopt the snow and ice defense.
lede: You went down on black ice in a parking lot that had been plowed and never sanded, or on something clear and wet in an aisle at the grocery store, and you got up embarrassed rather than angry. Three weeks later you are facing surgery on a wrist that will not heal straight, and the store has written to say its records show no notice of any hazardous condition. That phrase is not a throwaway. Notice is the hinge nearly every Washington slip and fall case turns on, and there are two well-established ways around it.

sections.heading: What a property owner owes you depends on why you were there

paras.p: Washington sorts people on land into invitees, licensees, and trespassers, and the duty changes with the category. A customer in a store, a tenant in a common area, and a member of the public in a building open for business are invitees, which is the category that gets the most protection.

For invitees the state follows the Restatement (Second) of Torts. In Iwai v. State, 129 Wn.2d 84 (1996), the Supreme Court set out section 343 and section 343A and cited Tincani v. Inland Empire Zoological Society, 124 Wn.2d 121 (1994), as having adopted them. Under section 343 a possessor of land is liable for harm from a condition if the possessor knows of it or by reasonable care would discover it, should realize it involves an unreasonable risk to invitees, should expect that invitees will not discover or realize the danger or will fail to protect themselves against it, and fails to exercise reasonable care to protect them.
That is a chain with four links, and a defense lawyer attacks whichever one is weakest. The first link is the one that becomes the notice fight.

sections.heading: Notice: what the owner knew, or should have known

paras.p: Iwai states the working rule plainly. In applying the knowledge requirement to premises liability actions, Washington law requires a plaintiff to show the landowner had actual or constructive notice of the unsafe condition, citing Ingersoll v. DeBartolo, Inc., 123 Wn.2d 649 (1994).

Actual notice means somebody knew. Constructive notice is the harder and more common theory, and the Iwai court described the plaintiff's burden as showing that the specific unsafe condition had existed for long enough that the defendant, exercising ordinary care, would have had sufficient opportunity to discover it.

So in a grocery store case the fight is about how long the spill was on the floor, and the evidence that answers it is almost never the plaintiff's memory. It is the sweep log, the inspection schedule, the camera that points at the aisle, and the testimony of whoever walked past it last. All of that is in the store's hands and most of it is overwritten or discarded on a schedule measured in weeks.

sections.heading: The exception that removes the notice requirement entirely

paras.p: In Pimentel v. Roundup Co., 100 Wn.2d 39 (1983), a paint can fell from a shelf onto a customer's foot in a self-service store. The Supreme Court held that where the operating procedures of any store are such that unreasonably dangerous conditions are continuous or reasonably foreseeable, there is no need to prove actual or constructive notice of such conditions in order to establish liability for injuries they cause.

The reasoning is that a business which chooses a mode of operation creating a foreseeable hazard already has notice of the hazard its own system produces. It does not get to require proof of notice of each particular instance of a risk it built in.

Iwai describes the same idea as the exception under which, if a specific unsafe condition is foreseeably inherent in the nature of the business or mode of operation, the plaintiff need not prove notice. In practice this is the theory that fits a self-service produce department, a drink station, a garden center, or an entryway that funnels wet feet onto hard floor every time it rains, and the way to make it is by showing the system rather than the spill.

sections.heading: Does an obvious hazard end the case?

paras.p: Not automatically, and this is the second provision most people have never heard of.

Restatement section 343A(1), quoted in Iwai, says a possessor of land is not liable to invitees for physical harm caused by a condition whose danger is known or obvious to them, unless the possessor should anticipate the harm despite such knowledge or obviousness. The Iwai court applied that directly, observing that the plaintiff may well have known about the ice in the parking lot, and framing the question as whether the defendant could and should have anticipated that she would encounter it anyway.

That is the real-world situation. A person who needs to get into the building, or into their own car, does not have the option of refusing the only route. Obviousness is an argument the defense will make. It is not the end of the inquiry, and the statute of comparative fault handles whatever is left of it.

sections.heading: Snow and ice: Washington declined to adopt the natural accumulation rule

paras.p: Iwai itself was a Spokane case. Over seven inches of snow fell on November 27, 1984, a contractor plowed the parking lot of a state office that day, apparently no sand was applied afterward, the temperature moved above and below freezing for two days, and the plaintiff fell on an inclined section of the lot.

The defendants asked the Supreme Court to adopt the natural accumulation rule for commercial parking lots, which in states that follow it precludes liability for injuries caused by naturally accumulated snow or ice. The court did not adopt it. It affirmed the Court of Appeals, which had reversed summary judgment and sent the case back for trial.

For anyone who falls on a winter surface in eastern Washington, that is the first thing to know. There is no automatic snow and ice defense here. Whether a given lot was maintained reasonably is a question the owner has to answer with evidence about plowing, sanding, inspection, and what the weather had been doing.

sections.heading: Being partly at fault, and the three years

paras.p: RCW 4.22.005 says contributory fault diminishes the award proportionately and does not bar recovery, so a finding that you should have been watching reduces a claim rather than ending it. RCW 4.22.015 directs the comparison to weigh both the nature of the conduct and how much it actually caused the damages.
The deadline is three years. RCW 4.16.080(2) sets a three-year limit for any other injury to the person or rights of another, running from the fall.

If you fell on property owned by a city, a county, a school district, a housing authority, or the state, there is a claim you have to present before you may file suit, and that deadline is much shorter than three years. The article on claims against government entities covers that step.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: Nobody writes to the property owner to preserve the video, and the system overwrites itself. The single most valuable piece of evidence in a store case usually has a lifespan of two to four weeks.

No incident report. Managers will often take one at the time, and a person who is embarrassed and in a hurry leaves without asking for it, which turns the fact of the fall itself into something that has to be proved.
No photographs of the surface. What the floor looked like, whether there was a mat, whether a cone was out, and where the lighting fell are all gone within the hour.

The case is built on the condition and never on the system. Notice is hard to prove one spill at a time and much easier to prove through sweep logs, staffing, and the design of the department, which is what Pimentel is for.
The fall is described in the medical chart as a mechanical fall with no mention of ice, water, or a floor condition, leaving no document that ties the injury to the premises.

Waiting. Weather data, maintenance contractor records, staffing records and video all age out, and in a snow and ice case the weather in the forty-eight hours before the fall is frequently the whole argument.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: The work that decides a premises case happens in the first few weeks and most of it is paperwork. Sending a preservation letter before the video is gone. Getting the incident report, the sweep and inspection logs, the maintenance contract and the snow removal invoices. Pulling the weather record for the days before the fall. Identifying whether the case is a notice case or a mode of operation case under Pimentel, because they are proved with different evidence and the choice is made early or not at all. Reading the lease where an owner and a tenant each say the other was responsible for the lot. And saying plainly whether the obviousness argument is a real one here, because under section 343A it sometimes is.

title: Wrongful Death in Washington: Who Can Bring It, What 2019 Changed, and the Second Claim That Runs Beside It
titleTag: Wrongful Death Lawyer in Spokane, WA | Justin D. Leigh
description: Washington's wrongful death statutes were rewritten in 2019 and made retroactive. Who the beneficiaries are now, why the personal representative has to bring it, and how the survival claim differs.
lede: Your brother was killed by a driver who ran a light, and in the first week the questions coming at you are about a funeral and a vehicle and a police report. Somewhere behind those is a legal question nobody has put to you yet, which is who in the family is actually allowed to bring a claim at all. Washington answers that by statute rather than by common sense, and the answer changed in 2019 in a way that opened the door for a great many families who would have been shut out before.

sections.heading: The claim belongs to the estate, not to the family directly

paras.p: RCW 4.20.010(1) provides that when the death of a person is caused by the wrongful act, neglect, or default of another, his or her personal representative may maintain an action against the person causing the death for the economic and noneconomic damages sustained by the beneficiaries listed in RCW 4.20.020, in such amounts as the trier of fact finds just under all the circumstances.

Read that carefully, because the first practical consequence is procedural. The person who brings the case is the personal representative. That means someone has to be appointed, which means the estate has to be opened, which takes time that nobody in the first month of a death is thinking about. A grieving spouse who hires a lawyer is not yet the plaintiff.

RCW 4.20.010(2) adds that the section applies whether or not the death was caused under circumstances amounting in law to a felony. A criminal case is a separate proceeding on a separate schedule, and whether it is charged, dismissed, or pleaded out does not control the civil claim.

sections.heading: Who the beneficiaries are

paras.p: RCW 4.20.020 sets the list in two tiers. The action is for the benefit of the spouse, state registered domestic partner, and child or children of the deceased, including stepchildren. If there is no spouse, state registered domestic partner, or child, the action may be maintained for the benefit of the parents or siblings of the deceased.

Two things in that sentence are worth stopping on. Stepchildren are named in the statute, which is not true in every state. And parents and siblings are a second tier rather than a parallel one, so the existence of a surviving spouse or child changes who the claim is for.

The same section closes by saying the trier of fact may give such damages as, under all the circumstances of the case, may to them seem just. Washington does not reduce the loss of a person to a formula, and the open language is deliberate.

sections.heading: What the 2019 amendments changed, and why they reached back

paras.p: RCW 4.20.010, RCW 4.20.020, RCW 4.20.046, and RCW 4.20.060 were all amended by the same act, 2019 c 159. Before it, Washington's second tier carried restrictions that kept many families out of court, and the amendment rewrote the beneficiary provision into the form quoted above.

The Legislature also wrote a retroactivity note into the act, which appears in the RCW following each amended section: this act is remedial and retroactive and applies to all claims that are not time barred, as well as any claims pending in any court on July 28, 2019.

That note is the reason to read older advice about Washington wrongful death with suspicion. A family told some years ago that they had no claim may have been told correctly at the time and may be wrong now, subject to the limitation period, which has not been suspended by anything.

sections.heading: The survival claim, which is a different claim about a different loss

paras.p: A wrongful death claim compensates what the beneficiaries lost. A survival claim compensates what the person who died lost, and in most serious cases the two run together.

RCW 4.20.046(1) provides that all causes of action survive to and against personal representatives. Subsection (2) is where the money is: in addition to recovering economic losses on behalf of the estate, the personal representative is entitled to recover noneconomic damages for pain and suffering, anxiety, emotional distress, or humiliation personal to and suffered by the deceased, on behalf of the beneficiaries enumerated in RCW 4.20.020. The subsection expressly says those damages are recoverable regardless of whether the death was occasioned by the injury that is the basis for the action.

RCW 4.20.060 is the special survival statute for a personal injury that occasions death. It provides that the action does not abate, names the same family tiers, and in subsection (3) allows recovery of the decedent's economic losses together with damages for the decedent's pain and suffering, anxiety, emotional distress, or humiliation.

The practical difference shows up in evidence. The survival claim turns on what the person experienced between the injury and the death, which is proved from medical records, responder narratives, and witnesses. Where that interval was minutes, it is still a claim, and where it was weeks it is a substantial one.

sections.heading: What is recoverable, and why Washington will not give you a number

paras.p: People ask what a wrongful death case is worth, and the honest answer begins with the fact that the statutes deliberately decline to say. RCW 4.20.010(1) allows economic and noneconomic damages sustained by the beneficiaries in such amounts as determined by a trier of fact to be just under all the circumstances of the case. RCW 4.20.020 closes with the same thought in older language: the trier of fact may give such damages as, under all circumstances of the case, may to them seem just.

Economic loss is the part that can be calculated. What the person earned and would have earned, the benefits that went with it, the value of what they did at home that now has to be paid for or go undone, and the costs the death itself created. That work is done by assembling records rather than by argument.

Noneconomic loss is the rest of it, and the statutes name the categories rather than scale them. On the survival side, RCW 4.20.046(2) and RCW 4.20.060(3) specify pain and suffering, anxiety, emotional distress, and humiliation suffered by the person who died. On the wrongful death side the loss belongs to the beneficiaries and is a different thing from the decedent's own suffering, which is why the two claims are pleaded together and proved separately.

Anyone who gives you a figure in the first month is guessing, because the economic analysis has not been done and the survival claim has not been developed. The number also has an outer limit that has nothing to do with the loss, which is how much insurance exists. That is a question to answer early rather than at the end.

sections.heading: How long does a wrongful death claim take to bring in Washington?

paras.p: The limitation period is three years. RCW 4.16.080(2) sets a three-year limit for any other injury to the person or rights of another, and a wrongful death claim runs under it.

Three years sounds generous until the first requirement is factored in. A personal representative has to be appointed before the action can be brought in the name the statute requires, and opening an estate is not instantaneous, particularly where there is no will or where the family does not agree about who should serve.

If the death involved a city, a county, a transit agency, a school district, or the state, a claim has to be presented before suit is permitted at all, on a much shorter clock. That is covered in the article on claims against government entities, and it is the single most common way a strong wrongful death case is lost.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: No estate is opened, and then nothing can be filed in the name RCW 4.20.010 requires while the three years run out.
The family treats the criminal case as the case. Restitution in a criminal sentence is narrower than civil damages by statute, and a prosecutor represents the state rather than the family.

Everyone focuses on the wrongful death claim and nobody develops the survival claim, so the record of what the person actually went through before they died is never assembled while the witnesses are reachable.

A beneficiary dispute inside the family goes unaddressed until there is money to argue about. The statute's tiers decide who is in and who is out, and knowing that early is kinder than discovering it at the end.
An insurer offers policy limits quickly, which can be the right answer, and nobody first checks whether there are other policies, other defendants, or an employer in the chain.
The government claim deadline passes while the family is still arranging a funeral.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: In the first month the work is mostly getting the right person appointed and preserving evidence that disappears. Opening the estate so there is a plaintiff. Identifying every beneficiary the statute names before anyone's expectations harden. Finding the vehicles, the scene, the employer, and the policies before any of them move. Preserving the medical and responder record that the survival claim depends on. Checking whether a government entity is in the case, because that deadline arrives while everything else is still being arranged. And handling the part that is not legal work at all, which is keeping a family from having to make decisions about litigation in the worst weeks of their lives.

title: Hit by a Drunk Driver in Washington: Negligence Per Se, the Bar That Served Him, and What Restitution Will Not Cover
titleTag: Drunk Driving Injury Lawyer in Spokane | Justin D. Leigh
description: Driving under the influence is one of the few violations Washington still treats as negligence per se. What that proves, when the bar is liable, why social hosts usually are not, and what criminal restitution leaves out.
lede: A driver crossed the center line and hit you head on, blew well over the limit at the scene, and is now facing charges. The prosecutor's office has been in touch about a hearing and somebody has mentioned restitution, and it sounds as though the system is handling it. It is handling the part of it that belongs to the state. The part that belongs to you is a separate case with different rules, a different deadline, and a category of loss that a restitution order is forbidden by statute to include.

sections.heading: Drunk driving is one of the few things Washington still calls negligence per se

paras.p: In most injury cases, breaking a traffic law is evidence rather than proof. RCW 5.40.050 says a breach of a duty imposed by statute, ordinance, or administrative rule shall not be considered negligence per se, but may be considered by the trier of fact as evidence of negligence.
Then it lists four exceptions that remain negligence per se, and the fourth is a breach of a duty relating to driving while under the influence of intoxicating liquor or any drug.

So in a case against a drunk driver, the negligence element is not the fight. That is unusual, and it changes what the case is about. The contest moves to causation, to damages, and above all to whether there is enough insurance anywhere to pay for what happened, which is why the next two sections matter more than people expect.

sections.heading: When the bar or restaurant is liable

paras.p: RCW 66.44.200(1) is one sentence: no person shall sell any liquor to any person apparently under the influence of liquor.

In Barrett v. Lucky Seven Saloon, Inc., 152 Wn.2d 259 (2004), the Washington Supreme Court took review on the single question whether RCW 66.44.200(1) establishes a standard of civil liability for damages caused by intoxicated drivers, and answered it in the affirmative. The trial court in that case had required the plaintiff to show the tavern sold alcohol to the driver when he was obviously intoxicated, which was the older common law phrase, rather than simply apparently under the influence, which is the statute's phrase. The court held that was error, reversed the Court of Appeals, and remanded for a new trial.

The difference between those two phrases is the difference between many of these cases being viable and not. Apparently under the influence is a lower threshold than obviously intoxicated, and it is the standard the statute wrote.

Proving it is evidentiary work done early. Receipts and point of sale records show how much was served and over how long. Server and bartender identities need to be fixed before turnover. Camera footage in a bar is overwritten in weeks. And the people who were drinking with the driver are the witnesses who can say what he looked like at 11:40, which is a thing nobody will remember in a year.

sections.heading: The private party is different, and usually not liable

paras.p: People assume that if a bar can be liable, the host of a party can be too. In Washington that is generally not so where the drinker was an adult.

In Burkhart v. Harrod, 110 Wn.2d 381 (1988), the Supreme Court was asked to extend to social hosts the principle that commercial furnishers who serve obviously intoxicated customers can be liable for damages caused by that intoxication. It declined. The court said that if social host liability is to be imposed in Washington it should be done through the Legislature, which has the greater ability to explore the competing interests, and held only that the judiciary is ill equipped to impose such a remedy. The trial court's summary judgment for the hosts was affirmed.

Two boundaries on that are worth stating rather than guessing at. Burkhart was about furnishing alcohol to an adult. Furnishing to someone under twenty-one is separately unlawful under RCW 66.44.270(1), which makes it a gross misdemeanor to sell, give, or otherwise supply liquor to a person under twenty-one or to permit a person under that age to consume liquor on premises under your control, and the statute defines premises to include real property, houses, buildings, motor vehicles, and watercraft. Whether and how that statute bears on a civil claim is a different question than the one Burkhart answered, and it is one to work through on the facts rather than to assume in either direction.

sections.heading: If you had been drinking too

paras.p: RCW 5.40.060 is the provision to understand, because it is harsher than ordinary comparative fault and because it contains a carve-out that most people never reach.

Subsection (1) makes it a complete defense that the injured person was under the influence at the time, that the condition was a proximate cause of the injury, and that the trier of fact finds that person more than fifty percent at fault. The standard for being under the influence is the criminal standard in RCW 46.61.502, and the statute says evidence meeting that standard is conclusive proof of the condition.

Subsection (2) is the carve-out, and it is squarely about this situation. In an action against the driver of a motor vehicle who was under the influence and whose condition was a proximate cause of the injury or death, subsection (1) does not create a defense even though the injured person was also under the influence, so long as that person's condition was not a proximate cause of the occurrence.

Read together: a passenger who had been drinking, in a car hit by a drunk driver, is not stripped of a claim by subsection (1) unless their own condition helped cause the crash. That is a narrower rule than the one adjusters describe.

sections.heading: Restitution is not compensation, and the statute says so

paras.p: This is where families are most often misled, and it is not a matter of interpretation. RCW 9.94A.753(3)(a) says restitution ordered on a criminal conviction shall be based on easily ascertainable damages for injury to or loss of property, actual expenses incurred for treatment for injury to persons, and lost wages resulting from injury. It then says restitution shall not include reimbursement for damages for mental anguish, pain and suffering, or other intangible losses, though it may include the cost of counseling reasonably related to the offense. The same subsection caps the amount at no more than double the offender's gain or the victim's loss.

So the category that is usually the largest part of a serious injury claim is excluded from restitution by the text of the statute, and the ceiling is set by the offender's gain or your loss rather than by what you actually need.

RCW 9.94A.753(9) is the other half of it: the section does not limit civil remedies or defenses available to the victim, the survivors of the victim, or the offender. The criminal case and the civil claim run alongside each other. Participating in one does not spend the other, and a restitution order is not a settlement.

sections.heading: Whether anybody can pay, which is the real question

paras.p: Drivers who cause these crashes are frequently uninsured, carrying minimum limits, or driving a car that belongs to someone else. A liability policy may also contain exclusions the owner has never read.

That is why the first document to find is your own declarations page. RCW 48.22.030(2) requires underinsured motorist coverage on auto policies issued in Washington, covering underinsured vehicles, hit-and-run vehicles, and phantom vehicles, and it is frequently the only coverage adequate to a serious injury. RCW 48.22.085(1) requires personal injury protection to be offered as an optional coverage on every automobile liability policy issued or renewed here, and RCW 48.22.085(2) permits a named insured to reject it in writing.

If the driver was working, or driving a company vehicle, or leaving a work function, there may be a commercial policy behind the personal one. Those questions get answered by investigation in the first weeks, not by waiting to see what the liability carrier offers.

sections.heading: How long do I have?

paras.p: Three years. RCW 4.16.080(2) sets a three-year limit for any other injury to the person or rights of another, running from the date of the crash, and it runs on its own schedule regardless of how long the criminal case takes.
RCW 4.16.190 takes out of the limitation period the time a claimant was under eighteen, which matters where children were in the car.
A claim for the death of a family member runs under the wrongful death statutes and requires a personal representative, which takes time to arrange. That is covered in the article on wrongful death.

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The family waits for the criminal case to finish, assuming restitution will handle it, and discovers at sentencing what RCW 9.94A.753(3)(a) excludes.

Nobody investigates where the driver was drinking. Receipts, server identities, and bar video age out inside the first few months, and by the time anyone asks, the Barrett theory is unprovable even where it was true.
An adjuster tells a passenger who had also been drinking that RCW 5.40.060 ends the claim, without mentioning subsection (2).
Nobody looks for a second policy. An employer, a vehicle owner, or an umbrella policy is often where the actual coverage is, and none of them volunteer.
A quick settlement with the liability carrier is signed before anyone asks whether it releases the underinsured motorist claim or whether consent to settle was required under that policy.
Treatment stops because of the cost, which both harms the person and hands the defense an argument about the injury having resolved.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: The liability case against the driver is usually the easy part, and that is exactly why the work goes elsewhere. Getting the breath or blood results and the criminal file. Finding where the driver was served, and getting receipts, point of sale data, server names and video before any of it is gone. Running down every policy that might reach the crash, including the ones on your own refrigerator door. Keeping your participation in the criminal case from damaging the civil one. And making sure nobody in the family signs a release in month two that costs them the underinsured motorist claim in month nine.

title: Collecting a Judgment in Washington: The Ten-Year Clock and the Ninety-Day Window
titleTag: Collecting a Judgment, Spokane WA | Justin D. Leigh
description: How long a Washington judgment stays enforceable, the ninety-day window for extending it, where it becomes a lien on the debtor real estate, and how to file a judgment from another state under chapter 6.36 RCW.
lede: You won, and then nothing happened. The judgment has sat in the court file for six or seven years because the defendant had no money and you had no appetite for chasing him. Now you hear he has bought a house. Or the judgment is an Oregon judgment and the debtor has since moved to Spokane. Either way the first question is not how to collect. It is whether the judgment is still good.
intro: A judgment is not money. It is permission to go and get money, and the permission expires. Most of what goes wrong in collection is not a failed levy or a clever debtor. It is a creditor who waited, and then found out that what he was holding had stopped being enforceable.

Washington keeps the rules in three places. RCW 6.17.020 sets how long you have and how to get longer. Chapter 4.56 RCW says when and where the judgment becomes a lien on land. Chapter 6.36 RCW is the route for a judgment entered in another state.

sections.heading: How long does a Washington judgment last?

paras.p: Ten years. You have that long to issue an execution, a garnishment, or other legal process to collect or enforce, counted from entry of the judgment or from the filing of the judgment in this state. RCW 6.17.020(1).

Then it stops. Ten years after the date of entry the judgment ceases to be a lien or charge against the estate or person of the judgment debtor, and no suit, action or other proceeding may ever extend the lien past that, except as the statute itself provides. RCW 4.56.210(1). Judgments for accrued child support and for obligations imposed in a criminal sentence run on their own clocks. RCW 6.17.020(2), (4).

sections.heading: What has to be done before the ten years runs out?

paras.p: This is the one thing on this page worth a calendar reminder. Within 90 days before the original ten-year period expires, the judgment holder may apply to the court that rendered the judgment, or to the court where it was filed as a foreign judgment, for an order granting an additional 10 years in which process may issue. RCW 6.17.020(3).

It is a window, not a deadline. The statute describes it in one direction, as the ninety days before the original period expires, and timeliness is one of the few things the court reviews. After the ten years there is nothing left to extend, because RCW 4.56.210(1) has already ended the lien and barred any proceeding to continue it.

The debtor has little to say about the application. It is granted as a matter of right, subject to review only for timeliness, full or partial satisfaction, or errors in the judgment summary amounts. RCW 6.17.020(3). It is not an occasion to relitigate the case. The order carries an updated judgment summary, and the filing fee is a recoverable cost.

paras.sub: The lien follows, and the trigger date can move

paras.p: Extend the judgment and the lien continues for another ten years. RCW 4.56.210(3). Perfection and priority are not altered and nothing has to be rerecorded, though a judgment transcribed to other counties stays perfected there only if a certified copy of the extension order is filed with each of those clerks. RCW 6.17.020(6).

A district court judgment transcribed to superior court is the trap. The original district court judgment is not extended, and the petition goes to the superior court within 90 days before the ten years expires, measured from the date the transcript was filed there rather than from the district court judgment. RCW 6.17.020(3).

There is also an outside limit, and one extension reaches it. Subject to the exceptions the statute names, no judgment is enforceable for more than 20 years from entry in the originating court. RCW 6.17.020(7).

sections.heading: Does the judgment accrue interest while I wait?

paras.p: Yes, and the rate depends on what kind of judgment it is. RCW 4.56.110 sets out categories rather than one number, so the first question is which category yours falls in.

A judgment founded on a written contract that provides for the payment of interest until paid at a specified rate bears interest at the contract rate, but only if that rate is set forth in the judgment. RCW 4.56.110(1). That proviso is worth checking against the face of your own judgment before assuming the contract rate is running.

Two categories are flat: twelve percent on unpaid child support, RCW 4.56.110(2), and nine percent from entry on a judgment for unpaid consumer debt as that term is defined in RCW 6.01.060. RCW 4.56.110(5).

Two are formulas against a published index. A judgment founded on the tortious conduct of individuals or other entities, and a judgment for unpaid private student loan debt, each bear interest from entry at two percentage points above the prime rate published by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System on the first business day of the month preceding entry. RCW 4.56.110(3)(b), (4). Where the tortious conduct is that of a public agency the formula is instead two points above the equivalent coupon issue yield on twenty-six week treasury bills, taken from the first bill market auction in the month preceding entry. RCW 4.56.110(3)(a).

Everything else takes the residual rule, which is a pointer and not a number: the maximum rate permitted under RCW 19.52.020 on the date of entry. RCW 4.56.110(6). And where a verdict was reinstated or affirmed on review, interest dates back to the date of the verdict rather than the date of entry. RCW 4.56.110(3), (6).

sections.heading: How does a judgment become a lien on the debtor's real property, and where?

paras.p: The debtor's real estate, including land the debtor acquires later, is bound to satisfy a judgment of a Washington superior court, district court, Court of Appeals or Supreme Court, or of a federal district court sitting in this state, unless the land is exempt by law. The judgment is a lien on it for up to ten years from entry. RCW 4.56.190.

Where the lien attaches is what creditors get wrong. A superior court judgment is a lien on the debtor's land in that same county from the time the county clerk files it on the execution docket. RCW 4.56.200(2). For land in a different county, and for judgments of the Court of Appeals, the Supreme Court, or a federal court sitting elsewhere, the lien runs only from the filing of a duly certified abstract of the judgment with the county clerk where the land is. RCW 4.56.200(3). A district court judgment gets there by its own route. RCW 4.56.200(4), (5).

So a judgment entered in Spokane County does nothing at all to the debtor's forty acres in Klickitat County until an abstract is filed with the Klickitat County clerk. If the debtor owns land in three counties, perfecting the lien is a three-county errand.

paras.sub: What the lien does not reach

paras.p: Personal property is not covered. It is held only from the time it is actually levied upon. RCW 4.56.190. And where the debtor owns land jointly or in common with someone else, the lien reaches the debtor's interest only, and only that interest can be levied on and sold. RCW 4.56.190; RCW 6.17.170.

sections.heading: What does filing a judgment from another state actually do?

paras.p: It puts the judgment on a Washington docket and makes it enforceable here as though a Washington court had entered it. An authenticated copy of the judgment may be filed with the clerk of any superior court in any county of this state, and the clerk treats it in the same manner as a judgment of a Washington superior court. RCW 6.36.025(1). A foreign judgment, for this purpose, is any judgment, decree or order of a court of the United States or of any state or territory that is entitled to full faith and credit here. RCW 6.36.010(1).

The equivalence is close to complete. A judgment so filed has the same effect as a Washington superior court judgment, carries the same defenses and the same proceedings for reopening, vacating, staying or extending, and may be enforced, extended or satisfied the same way. RCW 6.36.025(1). There is also a district court route, RCW 6.36.025(2), and either way the lien is governed by chapter 4.56 RCW and RCW 6.17.020, RCW 6.36.025(3), so the ten years and the ninety-day window apply to it too.

You are not required to use the chapter. It carries a section headed "Optional procedure," which leaves unimpaired the creditor's right to bring an action to enforce the judgment instead of proceeding under the chapter. RCW 6.36.160. Filing is the quick route, not the only one.

Interest on a filed foreign judgment follows the law of the state where it was rendered, not the Washington schedule below, and the court adds the cost of the authenticated copy and Washington court costs. RCW 6.36.140.

sections.heading: What has to be filed with it, and what can the debtor do about it?

paras.p: Two documents and a short wait stand between the filing and any enforcement. At the time of filing, the creditor or the creditor's lawyer files an affidavit with the clerk giving the name and last known post office address of the debtor and of the creditor, and the filing and expiration date of the judgment in the originating jurisdiction. RCW 6.36.035(1).

Promptly after that, the creditor mails the debtor notice of the filing at the address given, with the creditor's name and address and that of the creditor's lawyer in this state if there is one, and files proof of mailing with the clerk. RCW 6.36.035(2). No process issues until a period measured from the proof of mailing has run, which is ten days in superior court and fourteen in district court. RCW 6.36.035(3)(a), (b). Until the affidavit and the mailing are done and on file, the period that has to elapse before you can enforce has not begun.

Filing here also does not buy time the judgment no longer has at home. Nothing in that section extends the expiration date of a foreign judgment beyond its expiration date under the law of the jurisdiction where it originated. RCW 6.36.035(3)(c). The affidavit is where the court reads that date, which is why the statute asks for it.

Because the filed judgment carries the same defenses and the same proceedings for reopening, vacating or staying as a Washington judgment, RCW 6.36.025(1), the filing opens a Washington case. If the debtor shows an appeal is pending or will be taken, or that a stay of execution was granted, the court shall stay enforcement until the appeal ends or the stay lapses, on proof the debtor has furnished the security the rendering state required. RCW 6.36.045(1)(a). The debtor may also show any ground on which a Washington judgment would be stayed, and get a stay on the same security required here. RCW 6.36.045(1)(b).

sections.heading: What is execution, and how does it issue?

paras.p: Execution is the process that turns a judgment into a seizure. Within the ten years the holder may have an execution, a garnishment, or other legal process issued to collect or enforce the judgment. RCW 6.17.020(1). Execution produces a writ, the writ goes to the sheriff, and the sheriff is required to execute it without delay. RCW 6.17.160.

How the sheriff levies depends on what is being taken, and the statute prescribes a method for each kind of property. Real property is levied on by recording a copy of the writ, with a description of the property, with the recording officer of the county where the land is. RCW 6.17.160(1). Personal property capable of manual delivery is levied on by taking it into custody, and where it may be concealed in a building the sheriff may publicly demand delivery and, if the order of execution so directs, cause the building to be broken open. RCW 6.17.160(2).

Money held in court and intangible property each have their own method again. RCW 6.17.160(4), (7). A writ pointed at the wrong category is the usual waste. On a judgment filed under chapter 6.36 RCW, sale under the levy may be held any time after final judgment and not earlier, apart from perishable goods. RCW 6.36.130.

Garnishment of wages or of a bank account is the other common way a judgment gets enforced. It runs on its own statute, chapter 6.27 RCW, and how a writ of garnishment is obtained, served and answered is a subject in itself that this page does not take on.

sections.heading: How do I find out what the debtor owns?

paras.p: Chapter 6.32 RCW is the part of this most judgment holders have never heard of, and it is usually worth more than a speculative writ. At any time within ten years after entry of a judgment of twenty-five dollars or more, unless the time has been extended under RCW 6.17.020(3), the court may on the creditor's application order the debtor to appear before the judge, or a referee the judge appoints, and answer concerning the judgment. RCW 6.32.010(1). The tool lives inside the same ten years as everything else here, and rides the same extension.

There is a cheaper paper version. The court may instead order the debtor to answer written interrogatories under oath in a form the court approves, and taking that route waives nothing, because a creditor who uses it keeps the right to an examination in person. RCW 6.32.015.

It reaches past the debtor, which is the provision worth the most. Once an execution has issued and come back wholly or partly unsatisfied, any person or corporation can be ordered in and examined on proof that they hold personal property of the debtor worth twenty-five dollars or more, owe him that much, hold title to real estate for him, or simply have knowledge concerning his property interests. RCW 6.32.030. That last clause is wide, and it is how a creditor gets to question a bank, an employer, a bookkeeper or a business partner under oath.

The judge can also stop the property moving while this happens. An injunction order may restrain any person or corporation, party to the proceeding or not, from transferring, disposing of or interfering with the debtor's property, or with the particular property or debt someone has been called to be examined about, and it can issue at the same time as the examination order. RCW 6.32.120.

What you learn can be turned into money in the same proceeding. On affidavit proof that someone owes the judgment debtor, the judge may permit that person to pay the sheriff on account of the debt, up to the amount that will satisfy the execution, and may then direct the sheriff to apply it on an execution in the creditor's favor. RCW 6.32.070; RCW 6.32.100.

Appearing is not optional. A person who refuses, or without sufficient excuse neglects, to obey an order of the judge or referee or to attend on a subpoena may be punished as for contempt. RCW 6.32.180. A creditor who has served these proceedings is entitled to costs of service, notary fees and a twenty-five dollar appearance fee, plus reasonable attorney fees if the debtor fails to answer or appear. It runs both ways, and a creditor who starts the proceeding and then does not show up owes the appearing debtor the same. RCW 6.32.010(3).

What the chapter does not do is widen what you can take. It does not authorize seizure of, or interference with, property expressly exempt by law from levy and sale, property held in trust for the debtor where the trust was created by or funded from somebody other than the debtor, or the debtor's earnings for personal services to the extent they would be exempt against a garnishment of the employer. RCW 6.32.250.

sections.heading: What does the debtor get to keep?

paras.p: A good deal, and a creditor who has not worked this out before paying a sheriff is budgeting on a number that does not exist. The lien statute binds only real estate that is not exempt by law, and Washington exempts a lot.

The homestead is the real or personal property the owner, or a dependent of the owner, uses as a residence, and it has to be actually intended or used as the principal home. RCW 6.13.010(1). A mobile home can qualify whether or not it is affixed to the land and whether or not the lot belongs to the owner.

The exempt amount is not a flat number, and this is the part worth reading slowly. The homestead exemption amount is the greater of $125,000 or the county median sale price of a single-family home in the preceding calendar year. RCW 6.13.030(1). In a county where that median is above $125,000, the median is the exemption. A court determining it uses data from the Washington Center for Real Estate Research, or from a successor entity designated by the Office of Financial Management. RCW 6.13.030(2). There is also one narrow case with no dollar limit at all, involving another state's judgment for unpaid income tax on retirement benefits received while the person lived in Washington. RCW 6.13.030(1)(c).

Up to that amount, and except in the cases below, the homestead is exempt from attachment and from execution or forced sale for the owner's debts, and it is presumed valid to the extent of everything claimed until a creditor contests it. RCW 6.13.070(1), (4).

So the lien on a residence works differently from the lien described earlier. A judgment against the owner of a homestead becomes a lien on the value of the homestead property in excess of the homestead exemption, and it does so from the time the judgment creditor records the judgment with the recording officer of the county where the property is located. RCW 6.13.090. Equity below the exemption is not reachable, and the recording is what starts the lien on what is above it.

The exemption does not apply at all against judgments on certain debts, which is where a creditor sometimes has more room than it expected. Among them are construction, labor, material supplier and vendor liens against that same property, debts secured by a mortgage or deed of trust on it, child support and maintenance obligations, and association liens. RCW 6.13.080.

Chapter 6.15 RCW exempts a list of personal property from execution, attachment and garnishment. RCW 6.15.010(1). The items that matter in most collections are household goods, appliances, furniture and home and yard equipment up to $6,500, a motor vehicle up to $15,000, and the tools, instruments, materials and supplies of a trade up to $15,000. Wearing apparel is exempt outright, with a $3,500 ceiling on furs, jewelry and personal ornaments.

Then there is a general allowance for other personal property, outside bankruptcy, of up to $3,000, and the cash inside it is capped much lower. Of that $3,000, bank accounts, savings and loan accounts, stocks, bonds and other securities are limited to $500 for most debts, $2,000 where the debt is consumer debt, and $2,500 where it is private student loan debt. RCW 6.15.010(1)(d)(iii)(A). Part of each of those is automatically protected, which means a levy or a garnishment does not reach it even if the debtor claims nothing. Beginning July 1, 2027, those figures are adjusted and published every three years by the Department of Revenue to track the consumer price index for all urban consumers, rounded to the nearest $25. RCW 6.15.010(1)(d)(iii)(B).

Retirement money is close to untouchable. A pension from the federal government, and the right to a pension, annuity, retirement allowance, disability allowance or death benefit under an employee benefit plan, along with any fund created by such a plan, are exempt from execution, attachment, garnishment or seizure under any legal process whatever. RCW 6.15.020(2), (3). An employee benefit plan is treated as a spendthrift trust regardless of whether the debtor could withdraw from it. RCW 6.15.020(5). The exceptions are child support collection actions and certain state tax collection.

Two definitions do real work here. Value means the reasonable market value of the debtor's interest, exclusive of liens and encumbrances, so a financed car counts only for the equity in it. And each spouse is entitled to the exemptions separately, which means the figures above can double. RCW 6.15.010(2), (3).

paras.sub: How the claim gets made, and how a creditor tests it

paras.p: The debtor selects the exempt property, not the sheriff and not the creditor. RCW 6.15.060(1). A debtor claiming personal property exempt against an execution delivers to the levying officer, before sale, an itemized list of the property claimed exempt together with an itemized list of everything he owns, verified by affidavit, and the officer tells the creditor. RCW 6.15.060(3)(a).

The creditor then has seven days. A creditor who wants to object must give notice of the objection to the officer no later than seven days after the officer gave notice of the claim, or may instead demand an appraisement of the property. If those seven days pass with neither, the officer releases the claimed property to the debtor. RCW 6.15.060(4).

Against a garnishment the claim runs on a different track and a tighter clock. RCW 6.15.060(3)(b). The debtor may claim the exemption in the manner the statute creating it specifies, or by delivering or mailing a claim of exemption to the clerk of the court that issued the writ and mailing a copy to the creditor, no later than twenty-eight days after the date stated on the writ. RCW 6.27.160(1). A creditor wanting to object then has seven days from receiving the claim to serve a declaration of the facts behind the objection together with notice of a hearing, and that hearing must be noted for a date no later than fourteen days after the claim arrived. RCW 6.27.160(2).

That hearing carries a cost risk in both directions. The court shall award costs to the prevailing party and may award an attorney fee if it concludes that the exemption claim, or the objection to it, was not made in good faith, and the debtor carries the burden of proving the exemption, including documenting the source and amount of the funds. RCW 6.27.160(2). A creditor who decides not to object has ten days from receiving the claim to obtain and deliver a release to the garnishee, and failing to do that exposes it to fifty dollars on top of the debtor's actual damages. RCW 6.27.160(3).

sections.heading: Where this goes wrong

paras.p: The judgment runs out of time while nobody is counting. This is the big one. The file goes in a drawer because the debtor has nothing worth chasing, and the ninety-day window opens and closes years later with nobody looking at it. No court sends a reminder. The creditor who calls in year eleven because the debtor finally bought a house is calling about a judgment that is no longer a lien or charge against him.

A sister-state judgment is filed with nothing beside it. The authenticated copy goes to the clerk and that is treated as the whole job, with no affidavit, no notice mailed to the debtor and no proof of mailing. Since no process issues until ten days after the proof of mailing is filed, a bare filing is a judgment sitting on the docket that cannot be enforced, usually discovered when the writ is refused.

The extension goes to the wrong court, or is measured from the wrong date. For a district court judgment transcribed to superior court the petition belongs in the superior court and runs from the transcript date. A wrong trigger date costs the same as having filed nothing.
The lien is assumed to cover land wherever the debtor owns it. It does not, until a certified abstract is filed with the county clerk where that land is.

The house is treated as equity worth chasing before anyone has done the homestead arithmetic. The judgment reaches only the value above the exemption, and in a county where the median sale price is high there may be nothing above it at all.

Nobody finds out what the debtor owns. Every method of levy presupposes that you know which asset you are pointing the sheriff at, and chapter 6.32 RCW exists so that a creditor does not have to guess at it. A judgment, a willing sheriff and no asset information produce a bill and nothing else.

sections.heading: What a lawyer does here

paras.p: Most of it is dates and filings in the right order, and the dates are not where people assume. The ten years runs from entry for a judgment rendered here, and from the filing date for one filed here out of another state. A district court judgment moved up to superior court runs from the transcript date instead. Getting the trigger right is what makes the ninety-day window findable, and the window gets docketed years before anyone would otherwise open the file.

On the foreign judgment side the order of operations is the work: the authenticated copy, the affidavit carrying the originating dates, the mailed notice, the proof of mailing, then the wait counted from the right document. On the enforcement side it is working out which asset is actually reachable and by which method, and valuing the judgment as it stands today rather than as entered, since partial satisfaction is one of the few things a court looks at on an extension.

I am admitted in Washington, WSBA #55307, and in Oregon, OSB #242384, which is directly relevant here, because judgments cross that state line in both directions. I represent clients throughout Washington.

sections.heading: If you are holding a judgment that has not been collected

paras.p: If you are holding a Washington judgment and do not know how much time is left on it, or you have a judgment from another state against someone who is now here, my office offers a free initial consultation by appointment in downtown Spokane. Bring the judgment itself, or the county and the cause number, and the date it was entered, because that date is where every other answer starts.
